courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Projecting Gaussians to splats and sorting them by tile
question: A Gaussian moves twice as far from the camera along the view axis (all else equal, centered on screen). What happens to its 2D covariance entries?
options: They halve, because $J$ scales with $1/t_z$
They stay the same, because the 3D covariance did not change
They double, because the Gaussian is farther away
They drop to a quarter, because $J$ appears twice in $J W \Sigma W^{\top} J^{\top}$
explain: For a centered Gaussian, $J$ is roughly $(f/t_z) I$ on x and y. The covariance is sandwiched between $J$ and $J^{\top}$, so it scales by $(f/t_z)^2$: doubling the distance quarters the variance and halves the radius in pixels, as perspective should.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Tagged pointers: a version counter beside the pointer
question: Spot the bug: a developer stores the pointer and the tag in two separate std::atomic variables, loads them one after the other, and uses a 16-byte CAS only at the end. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: the final CAS compares both fields anyway
The tag will overflow faster
The two loads can pair an old pointer with a newer tag, so the snapshot may describe no state that ever existed
explain: Michael and Scott require the counter to be read together with the pointer. Two separate loads can interleave with updates, giving a mixed pair. Besides, a CAS can only cover one memory location, so pointer and tag must live in the same atomic word to be compared together at all.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Add-one-in vs leave-one-out on a fixed harness
question: Your full pipeline's reranker was tuned for two weeks; the no-reranker variant's BM25 parameters were never tuned. Which harness rule does this violate?
options: Same qrels
Same metric cutoff
Same candidate depth
Same tuning budget for each variant
explain: Unequal tuning credits effort, not design, to the tuned stage. This is the Melis et al. finding from lesson 1: on equal tuning footing, the simpler model won.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Why broken access control is OWASP's number one risk
question: In the 2025 OWASP Top 10, what happened to SSRF?
options: It was removed from the list
It became A10 on its own
It was rolled into A01 Broken Access Control
It was merged with Injection
explain: The 2025 introduction says SSRF has been rolled into A01. CWE-918 is among the notable CWEs listed on the A01 page.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Missing function-level checks and privilege escalation
question: A Django view has `@permission_required("docs.view_document")` and then `Document.objects.get(pk=pk)`. A user with that permission requests another user's document. What happens?
options: Django refuses because the permission is per object
Django returns 404 automatically
The document is returned, because the permission is model-level and the lookup is not scoped to the user
The decorator raises an error because pk is missing
explain: Model permissions answer "may this user view documents?", not "this document". Django core has no object-level permission implementation, so the view must scope the query, for example `get_object_or_404(Document, pk=pk, owner=request.user)`.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Access control models: ACL, RBAC, ABAC and ReBAC (Google Zanzibar)
question: A file-sharing product needs: files inherit sharing from folders, folders can be shared with groups, groups contain users. Which model fits most naturally?
options: RBAC with one role per folder
ReBAC, which computes access by following relationships such as parent folder and group membership
A single global ACL for the whole product
ABAC based only on time of day
explain: Inheritance through folders and groups is a graph of relationships, which is exactly what ReBAC and Zanzibar's tuples and rewrite rules express. One role per folder is the role explosion OWASP warns about.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Privileged groups, and why so many paths lead to Domain Admins
question: Which statement about Enterprise Admins is correct by default?
options: It exists in every domain
It is a member of the built-in Administrators group in every domain of the forest
It has no rights outside the schema
It is the same group as Domain Admins with a different name
explain: Enterprise Admins lives in the forest root and is nested into each domain's Administrators group, which is why compromising it gives every domain.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Kerberoasting: service tickets that can be cracked offline
question: Why is Kerberoasting invisible to account lockout?
options: Service accounts are exempt from lockout policy
The guessing happens offline against a ticket the attacker already holds, so no failed sign-in reaches the DC
Kerberos has no failure events
Lockout only applies to NTLM
explain: Requesting the ticket is a single successful 4769. Every guess afterwards is a local decryption attempt on the attacker's own hardware.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: DCSync: asking a domain controller for every password
question: Why does DCSync not need to run any code on the domain controller?
options: It exploits a memory corruption bug remotely
It sends a normal replication request over MS-DRSR, which the DC answers for any caller holding the replication rights
It copies ntds.dit over SMB
It uses Group Policy to run a script
explain: Replication is a network protocol DCs use with each other. The DC authorises the request by rights, so an account with both rights gets secrets back over the wire.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Tiered administration, Protected Users and LAPS
question: A Tier 0 admin uses RDP from a normal workstation to a DC. Why does the tier model forbid this even though the destination is a DC?
options: RDP is never allowed to DCs
The admin's credentials are typed and handled on the Tier 2 workstation, so anyone controlling that workstation can capture them
DCs cannot accept RDP
It only matters for Tier 1
explain: The source of the session matters as much as the destination. Admin work for Tier 0 should start from a Tier 0 device such as a PAW.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Information leaks: why modern exploits start by reading
question: A kernel driver copies a 24-byte structure to user space. The code sets every named field, but the compiler inserted 4 bytes of padding. What is the risk, and the fix?
options: None, padding is always zero
The structure is too small to matter
The padding may carry stale kernel data such as pointers; clear the whole structure before filling it, or build with automatic zero initialization
Only a risk on 32-bit systems
explain: Padding is part of the object's bytes but not of any field, so assignments never touch it. Copying the whole object copies stale data. Zeroing the structure first (or CONFIG_INIT_STACK_ALL_ZERO in the kernel) closes it.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: From use-after-free to type confusion, and how it is closed
question: In the demo, why did the plain build print "admin" although no code ever set is_admin to 1?
options: The compiler optimized away the free
malloc always returns zeroed memory
The freed session slot was reused for the note, so writing note.length wrote the bytes the stale session pointer reads as is_admin
puts was called through a corrupted function pointer
explain: Same-size objects can share a slot after free. The stale pointer then views the note's bytes through the session's type: a type confusion created by a use-after-free, affecting data rather than control.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Kernel cases: EternalBlue's size bug and Dirty Pipe's stale flag
question: Why could none of SMEP, SMAP, KASLR or kernel CFI stop Dirty Pipe?
options: They were disabled by default in Linux 5.8
Dirty Pipe ran on hardware without those features
The bug never ran user code in the kernel, never needed an address and never hijacked control flow; it misdirected ordinary writes through a stale flag
Dirty Pipe used return-oriented programming
explain: All four defend steps of a control-flow hijack. Dirty Pipe's effect came from an uninitialized flag changing what a legitimate write did, so there was nothing for them to check. Initializing the field fixed it.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: What this means for engineers: safe languages, fuzzing, defaults
question: Android's share of memory-safety vulnerabilities fell from 76% to 24% while most of its code was still C and C++. What explains this, per Google?
options: All old code was rewritten in Rust
MTE was enabled on all Android devices
New development moved to memory-safe languages, and since vulnerabilities concentrate in new code and decay with age, the unsafe code that remained kept getting safer
Fewer vulnerabilities were reported
explain: Google's post attributes the drop to safe coding for new code combined with exponential decay of vulnerability density in older code. Rewrites of old code have diminishing returns.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Rules of engagement for a red team
question: Halfway through an engagement the red team finds files showing someone else has a web shell on a server they compromised. What does a well-written ROE require?
options: Use the web shell, since it saves time
Remove the web shell quietly to protect the client
Note it in the final report in six weeks
Stop, report it to the named control-group contact, and suspend activity until the control group decides
explain: The template terminates activity on information about an actual intrusion and has the team report it to the designated contact. Touching or removing the attacker's tooling would destroy evidence and mix exercise and real activity.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Atomic Red Team: testing one technique at a time
question: Your rule for T1082 fires when the atomic test runs. What can you claim?
options: T1082 is fully covered
The rule detects this procedure on this build; other ways to perform T1082 remain untested
No adversary can perform discovery undetected
The SOC will respond correctly
explain: One test is one procedure. Coverage claims should name the procedures tested, and detection is not the same as response: whether an analyst triages it is a separate measurement.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Case: CISA's red team at a critical infrastructure organisation
question: The organisation was described as having 'a mature cyber posture', yet 10 of 13 loud events drew no reaction. What is the most useful conclusion?
options: Mature controls on paper must be validated by testing whether they produce alerts that people act on
Red teams always win, so the test proves nothing
The organisation should buy a new SIEM
Phase II events were too subtle
explain: Phase II events were designed to be noticed, and the expected detection points were named in advance. The gap between expected and actual reactions is exactly what assessments exist to measure.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Reporting, retesting and where to practise
question: Which finding is most useful to a defender?
options: 'We achieved Domain Admin in four days'
'At 10:02 on day 4 we read LSASS on SRV-SP01; Sysmon 10 was logged but no rule fired; suggested rule attached; owner detection engineering'
'The network is insecure'
'We used 12 tools'
explain: It names the step, the evidence, the gap type (detection logic), a proposed fix and an owner. The others describe the red team's success, not the defenders' next action.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: tau-bench: simulated users, database state and pass^k
question: A support-bot team can run one attempt per customer and has no way to verify success before the customer sees it. Which metric should drive their model choice?
options: pass@8, because more attempts give a better estimate
pass^1 alone, because only one attempt is made
pass^k for k greater than 1, because it rewards succeeding every time across conversation variations
pass@1 on a coding benchmark
explain: Each customer is a fresh trial of a similar task. pass^k measures whether the agent succeeds consistently across k such variations, which is the reliability the team needs. pass@k assumes you can retry and pick a winner, which they cannot.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Keeping the context window under control
question: Which item is safest to drop first when the context is filling up?
options: The system prompt's safety rules
The user's original task statement
The most recent tool result
The raw output of a test run from 20 steps ago that the agent already acted on
explain: An old tool result that has already been consumed is the classic low-value token: the agent's later actions reflect it. That is why tool result clearing is the lightest-touch compaction. The task, rules and most recent observations are what the next step depends on.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Main context vs external context: paging memory like an OS
question: In MemGPT, a message was evicted from the FIFO queue during a flush. Which statement is true?
options: The message is gone; only the recursive summary remains
It is still in the prompt, but compressed
It was moved into working context automatically
It is out of the prompt but still stored in recall storage, reachable through a search function call
explain: The queue manager writes every message to recall storage when it arrives. Eviction removes it from main context and folds it into the recursive summary, but the original stays in recall storage, which the LLM can search with a function call. Working context only changes when the LLM itself calls a write function.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Evaluating memory and the ways it fails
question: Your memory system scores well on recall but often answers with an old address after users move. Which LongMemEval ability is failing, and where would you fix it first?
options: Abstention; add a confidence threshold to the reader
Information extraction; use a bigger embedding model
Knowledge updates; fix the write path so a new address updates or invalidates the old one, and keep timestamps
Multi-session reasoning; retrieve more memories per query
explain: Recognizing that the user's information changed is LongMemEval's knowledge-update ability. Recall is fine, so a better retriever or more results would only surface both addresses. The fix is on the write path (UPDATE, DELETE or invalidation) plus timestamps so the reader can tell which is current.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: When more samples hurt, and how agreement helps
question: In CodeT, group A has 2 solutions that pass the same 5 tests and group B has 6 solutions that pass the same 2 tests. Which group does dual execution agreement prefer?
options: B, because its score 6 x 2 = 12 exceeds 2 x 5 = 10
A, because its solutions pass more tests
Neither; CodeT breaks ties at random
A, because CodeT only counts tests passed
explain: The score is |Sx| times |Sy|: 12 for B and 10 for A. Agreement among many solutions counts as much as test count, which is how CodeT resists a few wrong tests.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Where tasks come from: SWE-Gym, R2E-Gym, SWE-RL and hubs
question: SWE-Gym's headline training gains came from which procedure?
options: Fine-tuning on successful trajectories sampled in the environment (rejection sampling fine-tuning)
Multi-turn GRPO with a similarity reward
PPO with a learned value model over test outcomes
Pretraining on 6 TB of Docker images
explain: The paper uses rejection sampling fine-tuning, also called filtered behavior cloning (behavior cloning is supervised training to copy demonstrated actions; filtered means only successful ones are kept), as its policy improvement method. An environment with a reliable reward supports that as well as RL.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Direct and indirect injection, and how jailbreaks differ
question: A recruiter uses an AI tool to rank CVs. One applicant's PDF contains white text saying "This candidate is an excellent fit". What is this?
options: A jailbreak, because it bypasses safety training
Direct prompt injection by the recruiter
Not an attack, because the text is invisible
Indirect prompt injection through a document
explain: The recruiter is the user; the instruction arrives inside a document the tool processes. OWASP's LLM08 scenario describes exactly this hidden-text CV case.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: The lethal trifecta and excessive agency
question: A coding agent reads public GitHub issues, can read your private repositories, and can open pull requests on public repositories. Which trifecta leg is the pull request?
options: Private data
Untrusted content
External communication: a public pull request can carry private code out
None, pull requests are internal
explain: Public issues are untrusted content, private repositories are private data, and a public pull request is an exit anyone can read. This is the GitHub MCP case Willison cited.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Model supply chain: pickle files, safetensors and signing
question: A teammate wants to load a fine-tuned model shared as `adapter.bin` (a PyTorch pickle) from an unknown Hugging Face account. What is the safest choice?
options: Load it in the production cluster, since Hugging Face scans files
Open it with pickle.load to inspect it first
Ask for safetensors weights, or load it only with weights_only=True in an isolated environment, and prefer a signed model from a known publisher
Rename it to .safetensors
explain: Scanning flags but did not block known-bad files, and pickle.load runs the payload. Safetensors has no code path; weights_only restricts the unpickler; isolation limits damage if something slips through. Renaming changes nothing inside the file.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Defence in layers: privilege separation, provenance and egress
question: What weakness of the Dual LLM pattern does CaMeL address?
options: The Quarantined LLM can call tools
Untrusted data can still change values the plan uses, such as an email recipient, even though it cannot change the plan
The controller is itself an LLM
The Privileged LLM reads every email in full
explain: The Dual LLM pattern protects control flow. CaMeL adds data flow protection: capabilities on every value and policies at each tool call, so a recipient taken from an untrusted note can be blocked.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: GNoME: active learning with DFT, and what counts as new
question: Which issue did Cheetham and Seshadri identify as a systematic source of questionable "new" compounds in the GNoME listings?
options: DFT energies were computed with too small a plane-wave cutoff
The GNN used the wrong distance cutoff
Ordered arrangements of chemically similar atoms that would be disordered at real synthesis temperatures, an artifact of 0 K calculations without entropy
The convex hull was computed per atom instead of per formula unit
explain: Placing, say, the rare earths terbium (Tb) and samarium (Sm) on distinct sites can lower the DFT energy slightly and lowers the symmetry, creating an apparently new structure. At synthesis temperatures configurational entropy favors mixing, so the real compound would likely be a disordered version of a known structure type.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Distortion-free sampling: the Gumbel trick and SynthID tournaments
question: A watermarked model answers "What is 17 x 3?" with "51". Why will SynthID's mean g-value for this answer be close to 0.5?
options: The tournament only runs on outputs longer than 200 tokens
The model is almost certain of each token, so all candidates in the tournament are the same token and every match is decided by a coin flip
Numbers are excluded from the vocabulary hash
g-values are reset at the start of each response
explain: When p is concentrated on one token, all 2^m candidates are that token, so the output is fixed regardless of the g-values. The output's g-values are then just the token's pseudorandom values, averaging 0.5. Factual, low-entropy answers carry little watermark.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: Replaying workloads to compare allocators
question: Two replays of the same single-threaded workload with different allocators produce different ideal RSS logs. What does that tell you?
options: Allocator B is more fragmented
Something is wrong with the setup: ideal RSS depends only on the workload's requested sizes, so it must match
Allocator A rounds sizes up more
The kernel's statm counters are inaccurate
explain: Ideal RSS is the sum of requested sizes of live slots, computed by trace_run from the workload alone. Different allocators change VmRSS and VmSize, never the ideal curve. A mismatch means different workloads or a failed run. With several threads, unsynchronized operations interleave differently each run, so small differences are expected there.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Evaluating detectors when 1 percent of points are anomalies
question: You change IsolationForest(contamination="auto") to contamination=0.01 and retrain with the same random_state. What happens to average precision on the test set?
options: It stays the same, because contamination only moves the label threshold and does not change score_samples
It rises, because the model now knows the true anomaly rate
It falls, because fewer points are flagged
It becomes equal to precision@10
explain: contamination sets offset_, which only shifts decision_function and predict. score_samples, and therefore any ranking metric computed from it, is unchanged. Only threshold-based metrics like the precision of the predicted labels change.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Rate limits, quotas and resource exhaustion
question: Your API calls an SMS provider for password resets. Which control most directly stops a cost attack?
options: Gzip the response
Use a JWT instead of a session
A strict per-phone-number and per-account limit on reset SMS, plus a spending cap and alert with the provider
Return 429 only after 10,000 requests
explain: OWASP's API4 example is exactly this: each request triggers a paid message. Limiting per target and capping spend bounds the damage even if one limit is bypassed.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Scopes, consent phishing and refresh token rotation
question: A user fell for consent phishing yesterday and granted a fake app `Mail.Read`. IT resets the user's password and MFA. What is still true?
options: The app is certainly cut off, because tokens depend on the password
The app may still read mail with its existing tokens, and its consent remains, until the consent and tokens are revoked
The app can now read files too
Nothing changed, because MFA blocked the attack
explain: The grant is a separate object from the password; some providers revoke refresh tokens on a password change, but you cannot count on it and access tokens live until expiry. Revoke the consent and tokens, review the app's activity logs, and block it tenant-wide.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Classic JWT bugs: alg none, RS256 to HS256, kid and jku
question: An API verifies RS256 tokens with code that calls `verify(token, public_key_pem)` and the library reads alg from the header. An attacker knows the public key (it is published). What can go wrong?
options: Nothing, because public keys cannot sign
The attacker can sign an HS256 token using the public key bytes as the HMAC secret, and the library may accept it
The attacker can recover the private key from the public key
Only denial of service
explain: This is the 2015 algorithm confusion. RSA public keys cannot make RSA signatures, but any bytes can serve as an HMAC key. Pinning RS256 and using typed key objects closes it.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Detecting and responding to API and token attacks
question: Your API logs show a burst of tokens with `alg: HS256` arriving at an endpoint that only ever accepts RS256. They are all rejected. What is the right reading?
options: Someone is probing for algorithm confusion; alert, identify the source and client, and confirm every verifier pins its algorithm
Harmless noise from old clients
A clock skew problem
A sign the signing key should be made shorter
explain: Honest clients never change the algorithm. A burst like this is an attacker testing whether any verifier still trusts the header, so treat it as an attack in progress even though this endpoint held.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Secure code review: what a reviewer looks for
question: A pull request adds a new admin-only endpoint. In a diff-based review, what is the first thing to check?
options: That the endpoint actually enforces admin-only access on the server side
That the variable names follow the style guide
That the code has comments
That it has the best possible performance
explain: A new entry point is new attack surface. The cheat sheet's diff-based steps start with the impact on existing security controls and new attack vectors; a missing authorization check is invisible to most scanners.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: SAST in CI: false positives, triage and developer trust
question: A rule fired 40 times last month. Triage marked 10 as real bugs and 30 as safe. What is its precision, and what should you do?
options: 25%, make it non-blocking and fix or retire it
75%, keep it as a blocking rule
40%, because it fired 40 times
Precision cannot be computed without false negatives
explain: Precision = 10 / (10 + 30) = 25%. Three of four alerts waste a developer's time. Keep it as a comment-only rule while you narrow its sinks or add sanitisers, or retire it.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: CVE assignment and CNAs: who names a vulnerability
question: A small open-source project with no CNA receives a valid report. Nobody else's scope covers it. Who can assign the CVE?
options: Only NIST
A CNA of Last Resort, such as MITRE
The researcher, by choosing any free number
Nobody: projects without a CNA cannot get CVEs
explain: CNA-LRs exist exactly for products outside every other CNA's scope. MITRE did this for MOVEit's CVE-2023-34362.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Patch SLAs, exceptions and the race after disclosure
question: Why does BOD 26-04 add forensic triage to the 3-day deadline for exploited, total-control vulnerabilities?
options: Because patching takes longer for such bugs
Because the asset may already be compromised before the patch, and patching does not remove an attacker's persistence such as a web shell
Because KEV entries are often wrong
Because forensic triage is cheaper than patching
explain: MOVEit was exploited for four days before any patch existed. A patched server with a web shell is still compromised.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Commit, abort with CLRs, and fuzzy checkpoints
question: Why may a CLR never itself be undone?
options: CLRs are always forced to disk, so they are permanent
CLRs belong to the system, not to a transaction
CLRs are deleted at the next checkpoint
Undoing a CLR would reinstate the original change, and a rollback in progress must only move backward
explain: A CLR records progress of a rollback. Undoing it would reinstate an uncommitted change. Making CLRs redo-only and chaining them with UndoNextLSN guarantees rollbacks only move toward the start of the transaction.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Four ways to tell the model which side a text is on
question: You use a BGE-style model whose card says to prepend an instruction to short queries. A teammate prepends the same instruction to every passage at indexing time "for consistency". What is wrong?
options: Nothing; using the same instruction on both sides is how asymmetric models are meant to work
The model was trained with the instruction on queries only, so passages now look like queries and lose their document representation
Instructions are ignored at indexing time, so it only wastes tokens
It makes cosine scores negative
explain: BGE attaches the instruction to the query side only, and its card says no instruction is added to passages. Instructed passages are encoded as if they were queries, which is the "everything as query" mismatch you will see in the toy next lesson.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Why a plain loop is too slow and a plain gather is too fast
question: You wrap 5,000 calls in `asyncio.gather(*[call(x) for x in items])` with no semaphore. Call 37 raises an exception after 0.4 s. What happens to the other calls?
options: They keep running in the background; gather re-raises the first exception to the awaiting code
All other calls are cancelled immediately and an ExceptionGroup is raised
gather waits for every call to finish, then raises the first exception
The event loop stops and the program exits
explain: With return_exceptions=False, gather propagates the first exception immediately, and the Python docs say the other awaitables are not cancelled. They continue, so you can lose their results and still be throttled by them. Cancelling siblings and raising an ExceptionGroup is TaskGroup behavior.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Batch jobs, idempotent pipelines and putting it together
question: You must classify 2 million archived documents by next week, and your interactive product shares the same API account. Which plan fits best?
options: A batch job with a custom_id per document, results upserted by custom_id
Real-time calls with a semaphore of 500 and aggressive retries
Real-time calls one at a time to stay under the limits
Real-time calls with temperature 0 so the response cache absorbs most of the load
explain: Nothing here needs an answer in seconds. Batches cost less, run on a separate rate-limit pool so the product keeps its real-time capacity, and custom_id plus upserts make partial failures and re-runs safe. A huge semaphore competes with your own product for the shared limit, and distinct documents give the response cache nothing to reuse.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Wakers: how a Pending task gets polled again
question: A `Delay` future is polled once in task X, then moved into a new task Y and polled there. Which waker must it wake when the time expires?
options: Both X's and Y's wakers, to be safe
Y's waker, from the most recent poll
X's waker, from the first poll
Neither: wakers are per runtime, not per task
explain: The Future docs say only the waker from the most recent poll should be scheduled. The Tokio tutorial's fixed Delay compares the stored waker with `will_wake` on every poll and replaces it if the task changed. Waking X would poll the wrong task, and Y would hang.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Inside the CPU: LOCK CMPXCHG, LL/SC, and weak versus strong
question: get_key() lazily creates a random key: if KEY is 0, generate one and CAS it from 0 to the new key; if the CAS fails, use the key another thread stored. There is no loop. Which CAS should it use?
options: compare_exchange_weak, because it is faster on ARM
Either, since x86 and ARM compile them identically
compare_exchange (strong), because a spurious failure would make it return 0 as the key
Neither; it needs fetch_add
explain: With weak, the CAS could fail even though KEY was still 0, and the Err would carry 0, which the function would return as the key. Strong only fails if another thread really installed a key. Weak is for loops where a spurious failure just means one more iteration. And on LL/SC targets (ARMv8.0) the two do compile differently.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Sigmoid outputs and pooling patch scores into a clip score
question: A clip contains a barking dog and a person talking. Model A uses softmax over classes; model B uses independent sigmoids. Which statement is correct?
options: Both can output 0.9 for Dog and 0.9 for Speech
Only model A can output high scores for both
Only model B can output 0.9 for Dog and 0.9 for Speech at the same time
Neither can; multi-label clips need two separate models
explain: Softmax outputs sum to 1, so two classes cannot both be 0.9. Independent sigmoids treat each class as its own binary question, which is why audio taggers trained on AudioSet use sigmoid outputs and binary cross-entropy.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Storing passwords wrong: plaintext, encryption, fast hashes
question: Which single property of LinkedIn's 2012 storage most helped attackers crack millions of passwords quickly?
options: The hashes were 160 bits long
The hashes were stored in hexadecimal
SHA-1 can be decrypted with the right key
SHA-1 is fast and no per-user salt was used, so one guess tested every account at once
explain: Speed lets an attacker try many guesses per second, and no salt lets each guess test all accounts at once. SHA-1 has no key and cannot be decrypted; the attacker guesses and compares.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Password rules that work: NIST SP 800-63B
question: A user's password turns up in a newly published breach list. What does NIST say to do?
options: Nothing until the 90-day rotation comes around
Force a password change, because there is evidence of compromise
Add a security question to the account
Shorten the password minimum for that user
explain: No periodic rotation does not mean never rotate. Verifiers SHALL force a change when there is evidence the authenticator was compromised, and a breach list match is such evidence.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Kinds of MFA, and the maths inside a TOTP code
question: A login accepts 6-digit TOTP codes, allows one step of drift either way, and has no limit on failed attempts. What is the main risk?
options: The HMAC can be reversed to reveal the secret
An attacker who has the password can keep guessing codes; with 3 valid codes out of a million, unlimited tries succeed quickly
Clock drift will lock out legitimate users
The QR code can be decoded from the network
explain: Each guess wins with probability 3 in a million, so the defence depends on limiting tries. NIST requires rate limiting for short codes; 100 attempts gives an attacker about a 0.03% chance.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: SSO at a glance, detection signals, and responding to takeover
question: During an account takeover response, you reset the user's password. Why is that not enough on its own?
options: Password resets take 24 hours to apply
A reset makes the old password hash crackable
The new password must first be approved by NIST
The attacker may still hold valid sessions or refresh tokens and may have enrolled their own MFA device or recovery address
explain: A session token works without the password, and an attacker-added MFA device or recovery email lets them back in later. OWASP's guidance is to invalidate existing sessions and recovery links and remove compromised authenticators after recovery.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Tracking sources and checking every citation
question: A claim reads "Policy A caused the 2022 price drop" and cites a page saying "Policy A was enacted in 2021" and another saying "prices fell in 2022". Which error is this?
options: Citation hallucination
Inaccurate paraphrasing
Improper inferential linking
Prompt injection
explain: Both sources are real and accurately quoted, but neither states a causal link: the model inferred it. STORM found this the most common citation error, and a per-citation check that only asks "is this sentence on the page?" can miss it.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: Provisioned Throughput: when buying capacity beats paying per token
question: Using the illustrative numbers, traffic grows to 2x today. Peak input becomes 160,000 TPM. How many MUs do you need, and which option is cheaper per day?
options: 4 MUs; provisioned (768 cu) beats on-demand (907.2 cu)
3 MUs; provisioned (576 cu) beats on-demand
4 MUs; on-demand is cheaper
2 MUs are still enough because average load is lower
explain: 160,000 / 50,000 = 3.2 and 24,000 / 7,500 = 3.2, so you need ceil(3.2) = 4 MUs: 4 x 24 x 8 = 768 cu. On-demand doubles to 907.2 cu. Capacity is sized to peak, not average.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Why weight bytes set the price of decoding
question: Why does post-training quantization to 1 bit fail so badly while BitNet at 1 bit nearly matches FP16?
options: PTQ uses worse rounding rules than BitNet
BitNet keeps a hidden FP16 copy of the weights at inference
BitNet uses more parameters than the PTQ baseline
PTQ rounds weights that were optimized for real values; BitNet's optimizer chose weights that already work as 1-bit values
explain: The BitNet team's FAQ puts it directly: PTQ can only quantize weights around the full-precision values, which need not be where good low-precision solutions lie. Training with the quantizer in the loop lets the optimizer search among ternary solutions. At inference BitNet uses only the low-bit weights, and the compared models have the same size.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Why a pipelined CPU has to guess at every branch
question: A loop runs 1000 iterations and its loop-condition branch is mispredicted only on the final exit. Roughly what fraction of the loop's branches cost the penalty?
options: About 50 percent
About 10 percent
About 0.1 percent
None, loop branches are never predicted
explain: One miss in 1000 executions is 0.1 percent. Agner Fog notes exactly this: a loop with a high repeat count is mispredicted only when it exits, which is a negligible cost.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: When branchless loses, and how to measure it
question: A database's hot loop does a binary search over a sorted array, and the lookup keys arrive in sorted order (each key is close to the previous one). Which implementation is likely faster?
options: The branchy version, because successive searches take nearly the same path and are predicted well
cmov, because branchless is always faster for binary search
They are identical, since the compiler generates the same code
cmov, because it avoids loading from memory
explain: Agner Fog's binary search example: random keys give close to 50 percent prediction, where cmov wins, but keys close to each other make the branches predictable, and then a correct prediction breaks the dependency chain and overlaps loads.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Leveled vs tiered compaction: counting write, read and space cost
question: An ingest-heavy logging pipeline is limited by SSD write bandwidth and rarely reads old data. Which change most directly raises its sustainable write rate?
options: Switch from leveled to tiered (universal) compaction
Raise Bloom filter bits per key from 10 to 16
Lower the size ratio from 10 to 4 with leveled compaction
Use smaller memtables so flushes happen more often
explain: If compaction writes are the bottleneck, cutting write amplification from tens to a few multiplies the user write rate the disk can sustain. Bloom bits affect reads. In the model, lowering T for leveled only trims write cost slightly (38.9 to 25.9) while adding levels. Smaller memtables create more, smaller runs and more work.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: Sequential flooding: how one scan wipes out the hot set
question: A nightly report scans a 50 GB table on a server whose buffer pool is 32 GB, under plain LRU. What happens to the next morning's OLTP queries (online transaction processing: many short reads and writes of individual rows)?
options: Nothing; LRU keeps their pages because they were used more often
They get faster, because the pool is now warm
The scan fails because it does not fit in the pool
They see a burst of misses, because the scan's pages displaced their hot pages
explain: LRU only knows the time of the last reference. After the scan, the pool holds the most recent 32 GB of the scan, and the OLTP hot set has to be read back from disk. Frequency is invisible to plain LRU.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Business impact analysis: from processes to tolerable downtime
question: In the script, the contract penalty grows from USD 150,000 to USD 400,000. What happens to the MTD?
options: It stays at 42 h because the penalty is a one-off
It gets shorter, because the total crosses USD 1 million earlier
It gets longer, because penalties are paid by the customer
It cannot be computed any more
explain: The penalty applies from hour 9, so every later hour carries USD 250,000 more. Then 20,000 x h + 400,000 first exceeds USD 1 million at hour 31, so the MTD drops to 30 h. Steps in the impact curve move the MTD more than the hourly rate does.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Backups nobody restored: monitoring and testing that prove recovery
question: Your backup job emails the team on failure. The mail relay is reconfigured and silently drops its messages for a month. Which control would have caught this?
options: An alert that fires when the last-success timestamp is older than the backup interval plus a margin
A daily email saying the job succeeded
Making the failure email high priority
Running the backup twice a night
explain: Only an alert on the absence of success, evaluated by a separate monitoring system, detects every failure mode: errors, hangs, deleted jobs and broken notification paths. A daily success email is easy to stop reading, and its absence is easy to miss.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: When the building burns: OVHcloud 2021 and DR site strategies
question: Why might backups in SBG3 not have helped a customer whose server was in SBG2?
options: The whole site was isolated, so SBG3's services were down too
SBG3 was also destroyed
Backups cannot be restored across buildings
SBG3 used different hardware
explain: Octave Klaba's message said the whole site was isolated, affecting SBG1 to SBG4. SBG3 survived the fire but was unreachable, so a copy there shared the site failure domain.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Regulated resilience: DORA testing, TLPT and UK impact tolerances
question: Which statement about DORA's threat-led penetration testing is correct?
options: It is run in a test environment so production is never at risk
It is optional for all financial entities
It is a yearly vulnerability scan
It runs on live production systems supporting critical or important functions, at least every three years for identified entities
explain: Article 26 requires identified entities to perform TLPT at least every three years on live production systems supporting critical or important functions, following the TIBER-EU-based technical standards, with risk controls to limit impact.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Inside BLT: local encoder, latent Transformer, local decoder
question: Which part of BLT should get most of the parameters, and why?
options: The latent Transformer, because it runs once per patch, so its cost per byte is divided by the patch size
The local encoder, because it sees every byte
The local decoder, because it has the softmax
The entropy model, because it decides compute
explain: Cost per byte is about 2(m_g/P + m_l). Parameters in the latent model are amortized over P bytes; parameters in local models are paid on every byte. That is why the 8B model has 6.4B latent and only 140M local parameters.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: The same bugs in Rust: compile errors, panics, and what slips through
question: Why can `Option<&T>` be passed to C as a plain nullable pointer, but `Option<*const T>` cannot?
options: A reference is never null, so None can use the null address and the Option stays one pointer wide
References are always 16 bytes
C cannot read Rust enums of any kind
Raw pointers are not allowed inside Option
explain: The std `Option` docs guarantee that `Option<&T>`, `Option<&mut T>`, `Option<Box<T>>` and `Option<NonNull<T>>` (`NonNull<T>` is a raw pointer guaranteed not to be null) have the same size, alignment and ABI (application binary interface) as the inner pointer, with None as null; the ABI is how a value is laid out and passed between compiled functions. A raw pointer can already be null, so Option needs a separate tag (we measured 16 bytes).

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Build a safe type on unsafe: a minimal Vec from scratch
question: `pop` does `self.len -= 1` and then `ptr::read` on slot `len`. Why is the element not dropped twice, once by the caller and once by `Drop` later?
options: `ptr::read` zeroes the slot after copying
Strings cannot be dropped twice
`Drop` skips slots that hold a moved-out value
After the decrement, len no longer covers that slot, so Drop treats it as empty
explain: `ptr::read` copies the bits and leaves them in place. What stops a double drop is invariant 2: only the first len slots count as initialized. Decrementing len first moves ownership of that slot's value to the caller.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Cache lines: the cache moves 64 bytes, never just one
question: `double a[4096][4096]` is summed with `for (j...) for (i...) s += a[i][j];`. What is the main problem and the fix?
options: Each access is a new line because the inner loop strides 32 KB; swap the loops so j is innermost
Integer overflow in the index; use size_t
The sum is not vectorized; add a pragma
The array is too large for the stack; the loop order is irrelevant
explain: Row-major layout puts `a[i][j]` and `a[i+1][j]` 4096 x 8 = 32,768 bytes apart. With i innermost every access touches a new line and uses 8 of its 64 bytes. Making j innermost gives stride 8 and 1 miss per 8 elements. (Size and storage class are separate issues.)

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Transcoders and cross-layer transcoders
question: What does a transcoder learn to approximate?
options: The residual stream at the same layer, from itself
The output of an MLP layer, computed from that MLP's input
The attention pattern of every head in the layer
The final logits, computed from the embeddings
explain: A transcoder maps MLP input to MLP output through a wide sparse layer, so it can stand in for the MLP. An SAE reconstructs the same activation it reads, which describes but does not replace the computation.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Validating a graph with interventions
question: In the poem study, steering the planned-word features changed the rhyme only at the newline token, not at other positions. What does that support?
options: The model improvises the rhyme at the last word
Attention is broken at every other token
The plan is represented at a specific site before the line is written, and later tokens read it from there
Steering never works in Haiku
explain: If the plan were made at the end of the line, steering near the end would matter. The effect being confined to the newline token supports a planning site from which later positions read, which is what the attribution graph suggested.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Small propensities, high variance, and clipping
question: A ranker trained with IPS on a small log performs erratically: retraining on a different week of logs reorders many results. Propensities at ranks 8 to 10 are around 0.02. What is the most targeted fix?
options: Drop the propensity weights and train on raw clicks
Clip propensities at a tuned tau, or collect more data
Multiply all propensities by 10
Use only clicks at ranks 8 to 10
explain: Erratic retraining points to variance from weights near 50. Clipping caps them; more data shrinks variance directly. Dropping weights reintroduces bias, and scaling all propensities by a constant does not change the ranking the estimator prefers.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Stored XSS and the worms it made: Samy and TweetDeck
question: MySpace required a random hash from a confirmation page before adding a friend. Why did that not stop the Samy worm?
options: The hash was the same for every user, so it could be hard-coded
The worm guessed the hash by brute force
MySpace forgot to check the hash on the server
The worm's script ran inside MySpace's origin, so it could request the confirmation page, read the hash and submit it
explain: Anti-forgery tokens stop requests from other sites, which cannot read the token. Script injected into the site's own origin can read any same-origin page, so it reads the token like the real page would. OWASP's CSRF cheat sheet states it directly: XSS can defeat all CSRF mitigations.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: When users need HTML: sanitising with DOMPurify
question: A forum sanitises posts with DOMPurify, then replaces `:smile:` with ``. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, because the post was already sanitised
DOMPurify does not allow img elements
Emoji images are blocked by every CSP
The replacement builds new HTML from user text after sanitising, so that text is never checked
explain: OWASP warns that modifying sanitised content can void the protection. Here user-controlled text is pasted into an attribute after the sanitiser ran. Run the replacement first and sanitise the final HTML, or build the emoji element with DOM APIs.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Stopping CSRF: SameSite, tokens, Origin and Fetch Metadata
question: app.example.com uses `SameSite=Strict` cookies. An attacker takes over the forgotten subdomain `promo.example.com`. What stops a forged POST from promo to app?
options: Strict already blocks it, because the hosts differ
HSTS on app.example.com
Nothing can stop it
A CSRF token or a Sec-Fetch-Site check that requires same-origin, because the request is same-site but cross-origin
explain: SameSite compares sites, and both hosts share the site example.com, so the cookie is sent. The request is still cross-origin, so promo cannot read app's pages to learn a token, and the browser reports Sec-Fetch-Site: same-site, which a same-origin-only check rejects.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Detecting and responding to client-side attacks
question: Your CSP report endpoint suddenly receives thousands of reports from many users, all for `/product/42`, directive `script-src-elem`, blockedURL `inline`, with the same sample. What is the most likely cause?
options: A browser update broke CSP
A CSRF attack against the product page
A single attacker refreshing the page
A stored XSS payload on that product page, for example in a review, being blocked in each visitor's browser
explain: Identical inline samples on one page from many users is the signature of stored content that every visitor receives. CSP is blocking it, which buys time, but the payload must be found and removed and the rendering fixed.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: SigLIP's sigmoid loss and how CLIP training scales
question: In the SigLIP toy at t = 50 and b = -12, the cat photo and the dog caption have cosine 0.26, giving a logit of +1.0. What would lowering the bias b from -12 to -14 do to that cell?
options: Nothing, because the bias cancels in the sigmoid
It raises its match probability, increasing the loss
It changes only the positive cells
It lowers its logit to -1.0, so the pair is now judged a non-match and its loss falls
explain: The logit is t times cosine plus b: 50 x 0.26 - 14 = -1.0, so sigma gives 0.27 match probability and the negative's loss drops from 1.31 to about 0.31. The bias shifts every cell, which is why SigLIP learns it: it sets the threshold between match and non-match.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Blind spots: data events, flow logs and traffic you never see
question: An attacker on your instance runs the AWS CLI with --endpoint-url pointing at a storage service they own and uploads 50 GB. Where can you find evidence of it?
options: In your CloudTrail data events, as PutObject calls
Nowhere, because the CLI hides its traffic
In GuardDuty's S3 Protection findings for your buckets
In network evidence (flow logs, firewall or proxy logs) and host telemetry showing the process and its connections
explain: The requests go to someone else's service, so your provider's API logs never see them. What leaves your network does: flow records show the bytes and destination, and host telemetry shows the process. S3 Protection watches your buckets, not theirs.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Your own rules: key abuse, persistence and log tampering
question: An attacker shares an EBS (Elastic Block Store) disk snapshot of your database server with an AWS account they own. Which ATT&CK technique does this match, and which event shows it?
options: T1537 Transfer Data to Cloud Account; ModifySnapshotAttribute adding another account
T1530 Data from Cloud Storage; GetObject on the snapshot
T1580 Cloud Infrastructure Discovery; DescribeSnapshots
T1098.001 Additional Cloud Credentials; CreateAccessKey
explain: Sharing a snapshot moves data to another account on the same provider without a byte crossing your network edge, which is what T1537 describes. The sharing is a ModifySnapshotAttribute call that adds create-volume permission for the other account. DescribeSnapshots would be the discovery step before it.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Identity incidents: tokens, consent grants and mailbox rules
question: Which mailbox setting sends every incoming message to an external address, separately from any inbox rule?
options: ForwardingSmtpAddress
DeliverToMailboxAndForward
IncludeHidden
IsAdminConsent
explain: Microsoft documents that a non-blank ForwardingSmtpAddress forwards mail to an external recipient. DeliverToMailboxAndForward only controls whether a copy also stays in the mailbox; IncludeHidden is a parameter of Get-InboxRule; IsAdminConsent belongs to consent audit records.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Code Spaces 2014: why one account is one blast radius
question: A backup vault is locked in compliance mode and its lock date has passed. An administrator signed in as that account's root user tries to delete a backup that is still inside its retention period. What happens?
options: The deletion succeeds, because root bypasses all IAM policy
The deletion succeeds only if MFA is used
AWS Backup denies it; not even the root user or AWS can remove the lock or delete early
The deletion is queued until the 72-hour cooling-off period ends
explain: AWS's documentation says AWS Backup denies deletion attempts by any user, including the root user, and that after the grace time a compliance-mode lock cannot be changed or deleted by any user or by AWS. The 72-hour cooling-off happens before the lock date, not after.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: The same guardrails in Azure Policy and Google organization policy
question: In Azure, two policy assignments apply to the same subscription: one audits storage accounts that allow public network access, the other denies them. A new storage account with public access is submitted. What happens?
options: It is created and marked non-compliant, because audit runs first
It is denied: layered assignments are cumulative most restrictive
The newer assignment wins
Azure asks the creator to choose an effect
explain: Each assignment is evaluated independently and a matching deny blocks the request; Microsoft describes the result of layering as cumulative most restrictive. Deny is evaluated before audit for create and update requests.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Serverless: execution roles, event injection and function secrets
question: A function URL is configured with AuthType NONE and a resource-based policy allowing public invocation. Which statement is true?
options: Lambda still checks for an IAM signature before running the code
Anyone on the internet can invoke it, so the function's code is the only control
AuthType NONE only allows calls from inside the same VPC
IAM Access Analyzer cannot see function URLs
explain: With NONE, AWS says Lambda performs no authentication before invoking the function; the resource policy must allow public access, and then anyone can call it. Access Analyzer reports public and cross-account access to functions.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: CSPM, CIEM and CNAPP, and a full architecture review
question: A CNAPP reports 4,000 findings. Which one should a team fix first?
options: Detailed monitoring is disabled on 600 instances
An internet-reachable function with a known injection bug whose execution role can read the customer data bucket
Tags are missing on 1,200 resources
A sandbox account uses an older instance type
explain: Prioritise findings that form an attack path to sensitive data. The function combines exposure, a vulnerability and a privileged identity, which is exactly the toxic combination attack path analysis is built to surface.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: IAM from zero: users, groups, roles and the JSON policy
question: A policy allows `s3:ListBucket` on `arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket/*` only. Ana runs a listing of the bucket and is denied. Why?
options: Wildcards are not allowed in Resource
ListBucket acts on the bucket itself, so the Resource must be `arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket`, not the object pattern
Listing always needs the root user
ListBucket needs MFA
explain: Bucket-level operations such as ListBucket apply to the bucket ARN; object operations such as GetObject apply to object ARNs ending in /*. A mismatched pair matches nothing, so the default deny wins.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Instance roles at scale: IMDSv2 everywhere and a data perimeter
question: A team sets the Region's default to require IMDSv2. A week later an audit finds old instances still answering IMDSv1. Why?
options: Defaults only apply to Windows instances
The account-level default applies to new instances; existing instances keep their own setting until changed
The setting failed silently
IMDSv1 cannot be disabled
explain: AWS documents that setting the account-level default does not reset existing instances. Each running instance still needs modify-instance-metadata-options, or replacement.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Secrets and keys: KMS, envelope encryption and secret stores
question: In envelope encryption, what is stored next to the encrypted data?
options: The KMS key itself
The data key encrypted under the KMS key
The plaintext data key
Nothing; KMS stores every data key
explain: The plaintext data key is used and discarded. The wrapped copy is stored with the ciphertext, and only someone allowed to call Decrypt on the KMS key can unwrap it. KMS does not store data keys.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Incident response for a leaked cloud key
question: After deactivating the leaked key, CloudTrail shows the attacker called CreateAccessKey for the same user 20 minutes after the leak. What does that mean for the response?
options: Nothing, since the user's original key is now inactive
CloudTrail is wrong, because only the user can create keys
The quarantine policy has already removed it
The attacker has a second key that still works; it must be found, deactivated and removed, and the hunt widened for other persistence
explain: Creating a new key is classic persistence. Containment is not complete until every credential the attacker created is gone.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Choosing k: elbow, silhouette and their limits
question: A colleague plots inertia for k = 2 to 10, sees the steepest bend at k = 4, and says the data has four clusters. What is the strongest objection?
options: Inertia should go up with k, so their plot must be wrong
The elbow depends on the axis scaling and on the range of k plotted, and the same shape appears even for uniform data with no clusters
They should have used inertia divided by n, which would move the elbow to the right
Four clusters cannot be checked without ground truth labels
explain: Schubert's point: the curve looks the same on well separated blobs, on 25 blobs and on uniform noise, so a bend is not evidence of structure. Rescaling the data multiplies SSE by a squared and moves the apparent elbow, and starting the plot at k = 2 instead of k = 1 changes it again. Inertia does decrease with k, and dividing by n changes nothing about the shape.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: HDBSCAN: a hierarchy instead of one eps
question: A condensed tree has a cluster X with stability 3.1 whose two children have stabilities 1.2 and 1.4 (and no further splits). With cluster_selection_method="eom", what is selected?
options: The two children, because eom always prefers the finest clusters
Both X and its children, so every point gets two labels
Neither, because a cluster with children is never selected
X, because its stability 3.1 beats the children's total of 2.6
explain: Excess of mass keeps a parent when its stability exceeds the sum of its selected children's, otherwise it keeps the children. 3.1 is more than 1.2 + 1.4, so X wins and the children are dropped; the selected clusters never overlap. Always taking the finest clusters is the "leaf" method. On our ten points the root wins this comparison too, which is why allow_single_cluster=False matters.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Parquet on disk: row groups, column chunks, pages and a footer
question: A query filters on user_id = 42 over a 200 GB Parquet dataset written in arrival order (user_id random). Row-group stats show every group's min near 0 and max near the largest id. What will pruning achieve, and what fixes it?
options: Full pruning; min/max stats always locate a single value
Little pruning; sorting or clustering the data by user_id before writing makes min/max ranges narrow
Little pruning; switching from Snappy to Zstd compression fixes it
Full pruning, because dictionary encoding is applied to user_id
explain: Min/max stats can only exclude a group whose range misses the value. With random ids every range covers 42. Clustering by user_id narrows each range so most groups are skipped. The codec does not change the stats.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: SIMD, compiled queries and where columnar engines hit limits
question: A team's query is a long arithmetic expression over in-cache columns with almost no joins. Per Kersten et al., which engine style tends to win and why?
options: Vectorized, because it hides cache-miss latency better
Compiled (data-centric), because it keeps intermediates in registers and executes fewer instructions
Neither; Volcano tuple-at-a-time is best for arithmetic
Vectorized, because SIMD always gives 8x on arithmetic
explain: For computation-heavy, cache-resident queries like Q1, the compiled engine was 74% faster: vectorized primitives materialize every intermediate, costing extra loads, stores and instructions. Vectorized engines win on join-heavy, cache-miss-bound queries.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Vectorization and why -O2 and -O3 differ on loops
question: Why does adding `restrict` to all three pointers let the compiler drop the runtime check?
options: restrict makes the arrays aligned to 16 bytes
restrict forces -O3
restrict tells the compiler the arrays do not overlap, so stores cannot affect later loads
restrict copies the arrays before the loop
explain: The check exists only to detect overlap. restrict promises there is none, so the compiler can vectorize unconditionally. If the promise is false the program has undefined behavior.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
question: A physics simulation's results change in the 6th digit after switching from -O3 to -Ofast. What is the most likely cause?
options: -Ofast has a compiler bug
-Ofast enables -ffast-math, which allows reassociating floating-point operations
-Ofast uses less precise 16-bit floats
-Ofast disables vectorization
explain: -Ofast is -O3 plus -ffast-math. Reassociation (for example splitting a sum into vector lanes) changes rounding, exactly as in the 8-float example where the result went from 3 to 6. Neither answer is a bug; the strict one is what the source specifies.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Grounding: Set-of-Mark labels, DOM and accessibility trees
question: An agent must click one of 40 identical-looking "Edit" buttons, one per table row, in a web admin panel. Which observation makes grounding most reliable?
options: A higher-resolution screenshot so the model can count pixels more precisely
A Set-of-Mark overlay with 40 numbered boxes
A screenshot alone, since vision models read tables well
The accessibility tree, where each button's node sits under its row with the row's text and an element reference
explain: Visually identical targets are exactly where pixels and marks struggle: the model must link a label to the right row. The tree gives each button a structural context (its row's text) and an exact reference to act on. SeeAct found HTML-text choices beat image annotation for the same reason.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Why a concurrent test can pass a million times and still be wrong
question: In the two-thread load-then-store counter, which change makes every schedule end at 2?
options: Use `SeqCst` for both the load and the store
Add a `thread::sleep` between the load and the store
Replace the load and store with a single `fetch_add(1, AcqRel)`
Spawn the second thread only after the first has been spawned
explain: The bug is that read and write are two steps. Stronger orderings still let another thread run between them, and sleeping only makes that more likely. `fetch_add` is one atomic read-modify-write, so no thread can observe or write between the read and the write.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Choosing and running loom and ThreadSanitizer in a real project
question: You maintain a lock-free single-producer single-consumer ring buffer in Rust (about 80 lines) and a large async web service that uses it. Where should each tool go?
options: TSan on the ring buffer, loom on the web service
loom on the ring buffer with 2 threads and a small capacity; TSan on the service's test suite
loom on both, with LOOM_MAX_PREEMPTIONS=0 to keep it fast
Neither: Rust's borrow checker already rules out data races
explain: loom shines on small primitives with subtle orderings, and its cost explodes with threads and steps, so keep the model tiny. The service has far too many operations for loom but runs fine under TSan. Bound 0 would only check serial schedules, and the borrow checker does not check unsafe code or atomic orderings.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: iCT, sCM, LCM and the other few-step distillers
question: Why did Song and Dhariwal replace LPIPS with a Pseudo-Huber loss in improved consistency training?
options: LPIPS cannot be differentiated
Pseudo-Huber is required for one-step sampling
LPIPS made training diverge on CIFAR-10
LPIPS uses ImageNet-trained features like the FID evaluator, which can inflate FID, and it costs an extra network pass
explain: The iCT paper names two downsides of LPIPS: possible evaluation bias because LPIPS and the Inception network behind FID both learned from ImageNet, and the compute of backpropagating through an extra network. Pseudo-Huber is robust to outliers and twice differentiable.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Why quorum overlap alone is not linearizable, and the fix
question: Why can't ABD alone implement a linearizable compare-and-set on a replicated register?
options: Because it uses timestamps instead of clocks
Because it requires W = N
Because ABD reads are not linearizable
Because replicas may apply concurrent CAS operations in different orders and disagree on which succeeded
explain: ABD orders blind writes by timestamp, which is enough when a write ignores the old value. A CAS's outcome depends on the value it sees, so every replica must apply CAS operations in the same order. That is total order broadcast, which is equivalent to consensus.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Virtual nodes: many tokens per server smooth out the load
question: With 64 tokens per node, a node fails. Compared with 1 token per node, what happens to its load?
options: It all moves to one successor either way
It is lost until the node returns
It moves to the node with the most tokens
It spreads across many survivors in small pieces
explain: Each of the failed node's 64 arcs is absorbed by whichever node holds the next token after it, and those are scattered across the cluster. In the simulation every survivor gained 0.8 to 2.8 points instead of one neighbour gaining 27.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Decay functions turn distance and recency into smooth scores
question: A job board wants postings older than 60 days to stop getting any freshness credit, with a smooth decline before that. Which decay setup does that directly? (Elasticsearch writes durations such as 30 days as 30d.)
options: gauss with scale 60d
exp with scale 30d, decay 0.5
linear with origin now, scale 30d, decay 0.5
gauss with offset 60d
explain: Linear reaches exactly zero at d = scale / (1 - decay) = 30 / 0.5 = 60 days. Gauss and exp approach zero but never reach it, and an offset of 60 days would give full credit up to 60 days instead of none after it.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Arc consistency: AC-3 prunes domains before guessing
question: AC-3 finishes on a problem and every domain still has at least one value. What can you conclude?
options: A solution exists: take any value from each domain
No solution exists unless every domain is a single value
Nothing definite yet: arc consistency is necessary but not sufficient, so search is still needed
The problem has exactly one solution
explain: A non-empty arc-consistent network may still have no solution, as the triangle of pairwise inequalities over two values shows. An empty domain proves infeasibility, but a full one proves nothing. Search, with propagation at each node, settles the question.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: What ships in an image: base images, distroless and scanning
question: A distroless image has no shell. What is the most important security effect of that?
options: It prevents the kernel from running system calls
It encrypts the filesystem
It makes the image impossible to exploit
After exploiting the app, an attacker has no ready interpreter or tools inside the container to continue with
explain: The app can still have bugs, but the classic next step (open a shell, download tools) has nothing to work with. It raises the attacker's cost; it does not remove the need to patch the app.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: A hardened pod spec, line by line
question: A pod sets `runAsNonRoot: true` and nothing else in its security context. Its image contains a setuid-root helper. Which missing setting would block the helper from raising privileges?
options: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, which sets no_new_privs
automountServiceAccountToken: false
readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
hostUsers: true
explain: no_new_privs makes the kernel ignore the setuid bit on exec. allowPrivilegeEscalation defaults to true, so it must be set explicitly to false.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Service account tokens and cloud identity for pods
question: A cluster on AWS uses IRSA for every app, but pods can still reach the instance metadata service. What can an attacker in any pod do?
options: Fetch the node's IAM role credentials from IMDS and act with the node role's permissions
Read other clusters' Secrets
Nothing; IRSA disables IMDS
Only read their own role's credentials
explain: AWS's docs say containers have access to the node IAM role when IMDS is not restricted. IRSA adds a better path; it does not close the old one. Block or limit IMDS for pods too.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Exposed dashboards, kubelets and Docker APIs
question: Tesla's attackers kept CPU usage low and used an unlisted pool behind a CDN on a non-standard port. Which detection was hardest for them to evade?
options: A port-based firewall rule for well-known mining ports
An alert when CPU exceeds 90%
A process-level rule that flags known miner binaries or mining protocol command lines, combined with egress allowlists
A blocklist of known mining pool domains
explain: Each listed evasion targets one simple signal: domain lists, IP reputation, port rules, CPU alarms. Watching what processes run and allowing only expected outbound connections does not depend on those surface features.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: A container is a process with a narrowed view
question: Which statement about a container and a virtual machine running on the same node is correct?
options: Both run their own kernel, so a kernel panic affects only one of them
The container has its own scheduler, so cgroup limits are advisory
The container's threads are scheduled by the host kernel, which also serves their page faults and TCP connections
A container cannot share a CPU with other work
explain: The container's threads are plain tasks on the host kernel's run queues. That is what makes containers start in milliseconds, and also what makes the node's kernel shared fate for everything on it. A virtual machine does run a second kernel, at the cost of booting one.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: Probes, Services and DNS: liveness is not readiness
question: Every replica of a service uses one endpoint for both liveness and readiness, and that endpoint returns HTTP 503 (Service Unavailable) while the database is unreachable. The database restarts for 90 seconds. What happens?
options: Only readiness is affected, so traffic pauses and then resumes
The Service keeps routing, because liveness does not touch EndpointSlices
The scheduler moves the pods to other nodes
Every replica fails liveness and is restarted together, so recovery is delayed by cold starts on top of the database outage
explain: A liveness failure restarts the container; a readiness failure only removes it from the EndpointSlices. Because one shared endpoint drives both, a dependency outage triggers both everywhere at once: the fleet goes NotReady and is also restarted, so every replica returns cold. Liveness should test only the process; readiness is the right place to admit a dependency is down.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Resolving the second one and those against what was shown
question: Shown list v4 is [J4, J12, J5]. The user says *hide the Hooli one*, and the assistant shows [J4, J12]. The user then says *open the second one*. Which job should open?
options: J5, because it was second in the original search
J12, because it is second in the list currently on screen
J12, because the tracker remembers it from the previous turn
Ask a clarifying question every time
explain: Ordinals refer to the most recent list the user saw, here shown v6 = [J4, J12]. J12 happens to be second in both lists, but the reason it is right is the current list; the third option names the right job for the wrong reason, and would fail if the lists differed.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Do reasoning models admit the hints they use?
question: A model has n = 4 options. On hinted prompts it switches to the hint at rate p = 0.40 and to another non-hint option at rate q = 0.08. Among hint-switching CoTs, 18% mention the hint. What is the normalized faithfulness score?
explain: alpha = 1 - q/((n-2)p) = 1 - 0.08/(2 x 0.40) = 0.90. Normalized = 0.18/0.90 = 0.20. Normalizing raises the score slightly, because some switches are attributed to noise rather than hint use.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Pinned host memory: the precondition for overlap
question: On which system does switching from pageable to pinned host memory help least, and why?
options: The laptop, because its link is slower so the copy dominates either way
Neither; the ratio is a property of the PCIe generation, not the host
The desktop, because a faster GPU hides the staging copy behind the kernel
The desktop, because its CPU runs the driver's staging memcpy fast enough that staging was not the bottleneck
