options: The work item was already queued; the Arc that comes back is the reference the queue did not take, and dropping it is correct
The queue is full; retry in a loop until it returns Ok
The work item ran and failed; the returned Arc holds its error
Memory allocation failed inside the queue; the driver must free the Arc's memory by hand
explain: `queue_work_on` returns false when the work_struct is already pending, and the Rust wrapper then rebuilds the Arc from its raw pointer and returns it, so the reference count stays balanced. Enqueueing allocates nothing, and nothing has run yet.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Why the kernel lets a BPF program pick the next thread
question: Which problem does sched_ext mainly remove compared with patching CFS directly?
options: Scheduling decisions must be made in user space, which adds a context switch per pick
BPF programs run faster than compiled kernel C, so a fixed policy becomes cheaper
Each policy change needs a kernel rebuild, reboot, workload rewarm and fleet rollout, and a bug can crash the host
The fair class cannot run on machines with more than one L3 cache
explain: The motivation is iteration speed and safety: a policy is loaded and unloaded like a program, and the kernel can always revert to fair. BPF schedulers mostly run in the kernel (user space involvement is optional), and BPF is not faster than native kernel code.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Worked example: weighted vtime fairness in a few lines of BPF
question: You remove the clamp from scx_simple's enqueue. Which symptom appears first?
options: CPU-bound tasks starve each other in a round-robin cycle
A task waking from a long sleep wins nearly every pick for even longer than it slept, starving CPU-bound tasks
The verifier rejects the program because vtime can underflow
Nice values stop having any effect
explain: A sleeper's vtime stays where it was while running tasks keep advancing. Without the cap the waker is far behind and wins every pick it waits for until it catches up, which takes longer than the sleep because the others' vtimes keep rising: on a multi-CPU machine it runs almost continuously, hopping between CPUs, while the CPU-bound tasks share what is left.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Safety net, failure modes and schedulers in production
question: After switching a host to a sched_ext scheduler, a batch container's cpu.max limit is no longer enforced. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The verifier strips cgroup checks from BPF programs
cpu.max only applies to realtime tasks, which sched_ext does not handle
The kernel crashed back to bypass mode, where cgroups are ignored
cgroup CPU controls are passed to the BPF scheduler through callbacks and this scheduler does not implement them
explain: The kernel docs state the core reports cpu.max, cpu.weight and cpu.idle to the BPF scheduler via ops.cgroup_init() and cgroup_set_* callbacks, and each scheduler decides whether to implement them. Many ignore some of them, so read the scheduler's docs.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Hard-coded credentials (CWE-798) and why deleting them fails
question: Which of these is the inbound variant of CWE-798?
options: A mobile app that ships with the API key for its backend
A CI job that reads a token from the CI secret store
A script that reads a database password from an environment variable
A router whose firmware accepts the same maintenance password on every unit
explain: Inbound means the product checks incoming logins against a credential built into it, identical everywhere. The mobile app is the outbound variant. The CI job and the environment-variable script keep the value out of the code, so they are not CWE-798, though they have their own risks.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Splitting a key between people: Shamir's secret sharing
question: With a 3-of-5 split, how many shares can be lost or destroyed before the key becomes unrecoverable?
options: Any 2 can be lost; losing a third makes it unrecoverable
None
It is always recoverable from one share and the prime
explain: Recovery needs any 3 of the 5, so up to 2 may be lost. Choosing k and n trades availability (lower k, higher n) against the number of people an attacker must compromise (higher k).

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Key ceremonies: the DNS root key and multi-person control
question: Why does the root KSK use 3 of 7 Crypto Officers rather than 1 of 1 or 7 of 7?
options: 3 of 7 is required by FIPS 140-3
7 of 7 would be too slow for the HSM
Shamir's scheme only supports odd thresholds
1 of 1 lets one person misuse the key and 7 of 7 fails if anyone is ill; 3 of 7 needs collusion yet tolerates four absentees
explain: Threshold choice balances security (people needed to misuse) against availability (people who can be missing). FIPS 140-3 sets module requirements, not quorum sizes, and Shamir's scheme works for any k up to n.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: What a secure code reviewer is looking for
question: In a diff-based review, a new endpoint reads `request.headers['X-Account']` and passes it to a database query. Which question do you answer first?
options: Where the header value can come from and which sink it reaches
Whether the variable names follow the style guide
Whether the endpoint has unit tests for the happy path
Whether the query could be made faster with an index
explain: Headers are set by the client, so the value is a source an attacker controls, and a database query is a sink. Tracing source to sink comes first; style, speed and happy-path tests do not tell you whether a stranger can abuse it.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: JavaScript: prototype pollution and code built from strings
question: A team deploys with `--disable-proto=delete` and closes the ticket. Using the lodash case, what is wrong with that?
options: Nothing: without __proto__ there is no way to reach the prototype
constructor.prototype still reaches Object.prototype, as lodash's constructor payload did
The flag only affects browsers
The flag makes JSON.parse reject all objects
explain: --disable-proto removes the __proto__ accessor, but obj.constructor.prototype is another route to the same object. In our test the vulnerable merge was still polluted through it. Fix the merge itself.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Apple goto fail: one duplicated line in C
question: In the original goto fail code, why did the function report success after skipping the signature check?
options: The signature check returned success for every input
err still held 0 from the last successful hash update when control jumped to fail:
The compiler optimised the check away because of -O2
SSLFreeBuffer reset err to 0
explain: The jump happened right after a successful update, so err was 0, and fail: just returned it. The check itself was fine; it was never executed. The cleanup calls do not touch err.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Rust: what safe Rust promises, and reviewing unsafe
question: A crate exposes `pub fn get(&self, i: usize) -> &T { unsafe { self.items.get_unchecked(i) } }`. What is the review finding?
options: None: the code compiles, so the borrow checker proved it safe
The function is unsound: safe callers can pass any i and cause an out-of-bounds read
It should use a raw pointer instead of get_unchecked
It needs #![forbid(unsafe_code)]
explain: unsafe does not make the compiler check the precondition i < len; the programmer must. A public safe function that lets callers violate it is unsound. Check i < self.items.len() first, or simply use self.items[i]. forbid(unsafe_code) would reject the code rather than fix it.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Writing the finding and the fix so it gets merged
question: Which recommendation is best for a path traversal finding in a download endpoint?
options: Reject names containing ../
Resolve the final path and refuse it unless it is inside the download folder; better, look files up by id; add a test with ../ and an absolute path
Log a warning when .. appears
Add a WAF rule for ../
explain: Blocking one spelling misses absolute paths and encodings, and logging or a WAF rule only detects. Checking the resolved path (or not taking paths from users at all) removes the class, and the test keeps it removed.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: IKEv2: four messages to build the keys and the first tunnel
question: A responder receives thousands of IKE_SA_INIT requests per second from spoofed source addresses. Which mechanism lets it avoid doing Diffie-Hellman work for them?
options: The anti-replay window on the Child SA
Traffic selectors in IKE_AUTH
Switching IKE to UDP port 4500
Returning a COOKIE notification and processing only requests that echo it back
explain: The cookie is computed from a responder secret and the initiator's address, so only an initiator that really receives packets at that address can echo it. The anti-replay window protects ESP data, traffic selectors define what a tunnel carries, and port 4500 is for NAT traversal.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: SSH's transport layer: version, KEXINIT, key exchange and host keys
question: Why does changing a KEXINIT list in transit not let a man-in-the-middle downgrade SSH's cipher choice?
options: Because KEXINIT is encrypted
Because the client ignores the server's KEXINIT
Because both KEXINIT payloads are part of the exchange hash H that the server signs, so the client's check of the signature fails
Because sequence numbers prevent any message from being changed
explain: KEXINIT is sent in the clear, but H covers both payloads. The client computes H from what it sent and received; if the attacker changed either, the server's signature over its own H will not verify on the client.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Blast-RADIUS (CVE-2024-3596): MD5 collisions turn Reject into Accept
question: After patching, a RADIUS server sends Message-Authenticator in every reply, but the switches (the NAS devices) are not configured to require it. Is Blast-RADIUS mitigated?
options: Yes, the server-side patch is sufficient
Only for EAP logins
Yes, because the switches will see a Message-Authenticator and reject replies without it automatically
Not fully: a NAS that does not require Message-Authenticator can still accept a forged reply that lacks one
explain: The forged Accept simply omits Message-Authenticator. Unless the NAS requires it, the NAS validates only the MD5 Response Authenticator, which the collision defeats. The site's advice is to upgrade servers first, then clients, and set the require flags on both sides.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: VPN leaks and TunnelVision (CVE-2024-3661): routes beat tunnels
question: Why does a VPN kill switch typically not trigger during TunnelVision?
options: Because kill switches only watch DNS
Because DHCP disables the kill switch
Because the VPN's control channel and the route to the VPN server keep working, so the client still sees a healthy connection
Because the attacker stops the VPN process
explain: Kill switches react to the tunnel going down. TunnelVision leaves the tunnel up and steers other traffic around it; the VPN server's exception route still uses the physical interface as intended.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Biba and integrity: no read down, no write up
question: Why does Biba's strict integrity forbid a high-integrity subject from reading low-integrity data?
options: Because low data could steer the subject's actions and so corrupt what it writes to high objects
Because reading low data could reveal secrets
Because reading is slower across levels
It does not; strict integrity only restricts writes
explain: Integrity is about what you can rely on. A high subject that acts on low input can carry that contamination into high objects. Revealing secrets is a confidentiality concern, which is Bell-LaPadula's job.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Inside BeyondCorp: inventory, trust tiers and the access proxy
question: A laptop misses several OS patches. The engineer can still open the wiki but not code review. Which BeyondCorp component made that change, according to the 2016 paper?
options: The SSO system, by expiring the user's token
The RADIUS server, by moving the laptop to the guest network
The application, by checking the OS version itself
The Trust Inferer, by lowering the device's maximum trust tier
explain: The Trust Inferer analyses device state and sets the maximum tier; resources have minimum tiers, so the wiki (low minimum) stays available and code review (high minimum) does not. The user's identity did not change, and the application does not need its own logic.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Case: VPN appliances under attack, Pulse 2021 and Ivanti 2024
question: An agency patched its Ivanti appliances on the day updates appeared. Why did CISA still require resetting domain passwords twice and revoking Kerberos tickets?
options: Because the patch itself reset all passwords incorrectly
Because credentials typed through a compromised login page, and tickets issued with them, stay valid after the patch
Because Kerberos tickets expire too slowly to matter
Because the law requires annual password changes
explain: The attacker harvested credentials by modifying the login page and could have used them to obtain tickets and tokens. Patching the appliance removes the entry point, not the stolen access. Resetting twice and revoking tickets and tokens invalidates what was taken.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Running a security design review
question: A design gives an internal analytics service read access to the customer database and a direct network path to the payment processor, "for convenience". Which review question exposes the problem fastest?
options: Is the service written in a memory-safe language?
If this service is fully compromised, what can it reach and what secrets does it hold?
Does the service have a CC certificate?
Is the database encrypted at rest?
explain: Blast-radius thinking shows that one analytics bug becomes access to customer data and payments. Language choice, certification and encryption at rest matter, but none of them reveals the unnecessary path.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Idempotent steps: designing work that is safe to run twice
question: After a timeout, a worker retries a create-ticket call and generates a new uuid4 idempotency key for each attempt. What happens?
options: Each attempt looks like a new request, so if the first call actually succeeded, the retry creates a second ticket
The API rejects uuid4 keys
Retries become safe because every key is unique
Nothing changes: idempotency keys only affect GET requests
explain: The server can only recognise a retry if it carries the same key as the original. A uuid4 is fine as a key, but it must be generated once per logical operation and reused. Stripe notes GET and DELETE are idempotent by definition, so keys there have no effect.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: LLMs from zero: tokens, sampling and confident mistakes
question: Your triage prompt, run 10 times at temperature 0 on the same alert, says likely_benign 9 times and likely_malicious once. What does that tell you?
options: The model is broken and should be replaced
Temperature 0 guarantees identical output, so the alert must have changed
Outputs are not fixed even at temperature 0: measure over repeated runs, and never let a single sample decide
The alert is 90% benign
explain: Inference is not fully deterministic in practice, as the Thinking Machines experiment showed. A vote of 9 to 1 is a property of the model and prompt, not a probability that the alert is benign.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: AI for finding bugs, reviewing code and writing detections
question: What made the Big Sleep and AIxCC results credible?
options: Each claim came with machine-checkable evidence: a reproducing input, a crash or a patch that passes tests
The models were very large
The vendors said so
They used the lowest temperature
explain: Verification, not model size or confidence, is what separates a finding from slop. The same standard applies to AI-written detections and code review comments.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Attack surface, and the Morris worm's four doors
question: Which Morris worm door involved no programming bug at all?
options: Trusted-hosts logins and guessable passwords
fingerd reading input with gets()
sendmail's debug command
None: every door was a coding error
explain: Trusted hosts worked exactly as designed, and weak passwords are a human choice. Attack surface includes features and people, not just bugs. The fingerd and sendmail doors were implementation errors.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: EternalBlue and WannaCry: a patch, a leak and a worm
question: An organisation cannot patch an old Windows Server this week. Which CISA fallback reduces the risk most?
options: Disable SMBv1 and block SMB ports at the network boundary
Turn off Windows Update
Rename the server
Pay for a larger internet connection
explain: CISA recommended disabling SMBv1 and blocking TCP 445 and related ports at the boundary when the patch could not be applied. This removes or hides the vulnerable code path.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Who does security work: the job families
question: In the SSH pipeline, why match `from [0-9.]+` instead of taking a fixed word position with awk on the whole line?
options: Because lines for nonexistent users contain two extra words ('invalid user'), so the address is not always in the same position
Because grep is faster than awk
Because awk cannot read log files
Because IP addresses are encrypted in the log
explain: The 'invalid user' variant shifts every later field by two. Matching the text right after 'from' finds the address in both formats.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Severity you can defend: scores, context and confidence
question: A report says only: "Severity: 9.8". What is the most important thing missing?
options: Which scale and version produced it (for example CVSS 3.1 base) and whether it was adjusted for this environment
Nothing; 9.8 is clear
The colour of the severity badge
The name of the tester
explain: The CVSS 4.0 specification asks for nomenclature (CVSS-B, BT, BE, BTE) wherever a number appears, because the same bug scores differently by version and by which metric groups were used.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Incident updates when you do not know yet
question: Which incident update sentence best states uncertainty?
options: We judge it unlikely (about 30%) that customer data was accessed; this rests on 60% of logs reviewed, and we expect a firmer answer by 16:00.
The attacker definitely did not reach customer data.
Customer data may have potentially been impacted in some way.
We cannot comment during an investigation.
explain: It gives a word with a number, the basis for the judgement, and when it will improve. 'Definitely did not' overstates, 'may have potentially' is vague, and 'cannot comment' gives readers nothing to plan with.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Presenting to a board: risk, money and decisions
question: Which slide title is best for a board?
options: Ransomware could stop order fulfilment for about 5 days; target 2; closing the gap needs the backup budget on today's agenda
Firewall dropped 4.2M packets from 37 countries
We are fully compliant with all frameworks
Top 10 CVEs this quarter
explain: It names a business outcome, a measured current state, a target and the decision needed. The others are activity, an unfalsifiable claim, or technical detail directors cannot act on.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: When the filter lies: lucky answers, proxy rewards, overfitting
question: For which task would a STaR-style final-answer filter keep the fewest flawed rationales, for the same model accuracy?
options: True or false questions
5-way multiple choice questions
Competition math problems with an integer answer
Open-ended summaries scored by a learned reward model
explain: The flawed share depends on c, the chance a flawed attempt matches anyway. It is 0.5 for true or false, 0.2 for 5 options, and tiny for an integer answer. A learned reward model adds its own errors on top, as ReST's human evaluation showed.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Choosing the threshold: hit rate against false hits
question: Which pair is most likely to produce a false hit with a plain embedding similarity threshold?
options: "Do you ship to Canada?" and "Do you ship to Mexico?"
"Do you ship to Canada?" and "Can I get delivery in Canada?"
"How do I reset my password?" and "What is your return policy?"
"What are your opening hours?" and "When are you open?"
explain: Swapping one entity keeps the sentence nearly identical, so the embeddings stay very close while the correct answer changes. The second and fourth pairs are true paraphrases, and the third pair is far apart and will simply miss.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: The server as a confused deputy
question: A PDF export feature renders a user-supplied HTML page on the server, including any images the HTML references. Which confused-deputy risk does this create most directly?
options: Cross-site scripting in the user's browser
The server fetches image URLs the user chose, so it can be pointed at internal hosts (SSRF)
SQL injection in the PDF library
None: PDFs are static files
explain: The renderer fetches every URL the HTML names, from the server's network position. That is SSRF through a feature that does not look like a URL fetcher. OWASP's SSRF cheat sheet gives user-supplied image URLs and webhooks as typical entry points; a document renderer that loads remote images is the same pattern.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Egress filtering, isolation and detecting SSRF
question: Why is an alert on VPC Flow Logs records for 169.254.169.254 not a working detection for metadata SSRF on AWS?
options: Flow logs are encrypted
AWS documents that flow logs do not record traffic to and from the instance metadata address at all
Flow logs only exist for IPv6
The metadata service uses UDP
explain: Metadata traffic never appears in flow logs, so an alert on it can never fire. Use the IMDS CloudWatch metrics, host-level monitoring and credential-use signals (CloudTrail, GuardDuty) instead.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Log4Shell response: versions, mitigations and detection
question: A server running a vulnerable Log4j sits behind a firewall that denies all outbound connections except to its database. An attacker sends the lookup string. What is the most likely result?
options: Full remote code execution as usual
The lookup triggers an outbound connection attempt that the firewall denies, so the chain breaks and the denied connection shows up in firewall logs
The database is compromised instead
Nothing at all is logged anywhere
explain: The classic chain needs an outbound connection to the attacker's directory server. Default-deny egress breaks it and produces a denial log entry, which is excellent evidence. Patch anyway: lookups that read local data, such as environment variables, can still leak them into logs.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: When front end and back end disagree: smuggling and ProxyLogon
question: In ProxyLogon, why did the back end perform privileged actions for an unauthenticated attacker?
options: The attacker cracked an admin password
Exchange had no back end
The front end forwarded the attacker-routed request using the Exchange server's own Kerberos identity, which the back end trusted
The attacker used request smuggling
explain: The front end lent its own credentials to a request whose destination the attacker chose: SSRF with a confused deputy. The fix validated the routing value as a host name and stopped the front end from authenticating such requests as itself.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Inside the server: three processes and an overlapped loop
question: Why can't the scheduler simply build batch k+1 while batch k runs, with no extra machinery?
options: Batch k+1 needs batch k's sampled tokens as its inputs, which are not known until batch k finishes; SGLang uses future-token placeholders resolved on the GPU
The GPU cannot run two kernels in a row
Python cannot start a second thread
The radix tree must be rebuilt from scratch every step
explain: For decoding, each step's input is the previous step's output. Overlap therefore needs a way to refer to tokens that do not exist yet. The release notes describe resolving this dependency with future tokens and careful CUDA event synchronization.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: A*: steering the search with a lower bound
question: To speed things up, someone divides straight-line km by 30 km/h instead of the network's top speed of 60 km/h. What is the risk?
options: None; any distance-based estimate keeps A* optimal
A* will settle more nodes than before
The heuristic may now overestimate on fast roads, so A* can return a slower route than the optimum
The algorithm may loop forever
explain: At 30 km/h each kilometer is estimated at 2 minutes, but a 60 km/h road covers it in 1. Overestimating breaks Theorem 1's condition, so optimality is no longer guaranteed. The survey notes such aggressive bounds speed things up only by giving up correctness.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: Frequency bins, resolution and spectral leakage
question: You record 2 s of data at 1000 Hz and need to tell apart tones at 50.0 Hz and 50.3 Hz. What helps?
options: Zero-pad to 8 times the length before the FFT
Sample at 4000 Hz instead of 1000 Hz for the same 2 s
Record for longer: at least several seconds, since the bin spacing is 1/duration
Apply a Hann window, which sharpens peaks
explain: Resolution is fs/N = 1/duration. Two seconds gives 0.5 Hz bins, too coarse for a 0.3 Hz gap; you need more than 1/0.3 = 3.3 s, and more still with a window, which widens peaks. A higher fs adds bins at high frequencies but keeps the spacing at 1/duration. Zero-padding only interpolates the same blurred spectrum.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Writing a vector loop: intrinsics, reductions and tails
question: You remove the scalar tail loop from sum_avx2 to save code. What happens for n = 19?
options: Nothing, the vector loop reads all 19 elements
It returns 136, silently dropping a[16], a[17] and a[18]
It crashes because the last load is out of bounds
It returns 190 but more slowly
explain: The vector loop stops at i = 16 because 16 + 8 > 19, so it never reads past the end. Without the tail the last 3 elements are never added: you get 136 instead of 190. Silent wrong answers like this are the classic SIMD bug.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Shipping SIMD: -march levels, runtime dispatch, portability
question: You ship a desktop app built with `-march=x86-64-v4` because benchmarks on your AVX-512 workstation looked great. Users with AVX2-only laptops report crashes at startup. What is the right fix?
options: Add -O3
Build for the baseline or x86-64-v3 and use target_clones or runtime checks for the AVX-512 hot loops
Switch to -ffast-math
Catch SIGILL and retry
explain: x86-64-v4 lets the compiler place AVX-512 instructions anywhere, including startup code. Build the bulk for a level every user has, and multiversion only the hot kernels so each CPU picks its best copy.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: The slab allocator: caches of ready-made objects
question: A slab holds 31 objects of 128 bytes in a 4096-byte page, with 32 bytes of in-page metadata. Without coloring, every slab's objects start at offset 0. What does coloring change?
options: It fits a 32nd object into the page by moving the metadata elsewhere
It uses the 96 leftover bytes to start each new slab's objects at a different offset, so hot fields of objects in different slabs map to different cache sets
It rounds the objects up to 256 bytes so each one is cache-line aligned
It marks freed objects with a pattern so use-after-free is detected
explain: 31 x 128 = 3968 bytes, plus 32 metadata leaves 96 spare bytes. Coloring spends that otherwise wasted space on an offset that varies per slab. (Filling freed memory with 0xdeadbeef is a separate debugging feature.)

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Moving weights from Megatron into SGLang
question: You move a working colocated job to separate pools and add `--update-weight-mode delta` but keep the default transport. What happens?
options: It fails an assertion: delta mode requires `--update-weight-transport disk`
It runs, shipping deltas over NCCL
It silently falls back to full NCCL sync
It uses CUDA IPC because the engines are on the same nodes
explain: `create_weight_updater` asserts that delta mode uses disk transport (and is not colocated). Delta sync works by publishing versioned checkpoint directories that engines pull, not by broadcasting.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: What a SOC is, and what an analyst does all day
question: Which handover note is most useful to the next shift?
options: "Quiet night, a few alerts, all handled"
A list of every alert ID closed during the shift
"C-311: waiting on user reply since 05:40; if none by 09:00, revoke sessions. Proxy logs silent since 02:00, ticket P-88"
"Ask me if anything comes up"
explain: The next shift needs open items, what each is blocked on, the next step with a deadline, and environmental changes such as a dead log source. A list of closed IDs or a vague summary gives them nothing to act on, and the author may be asleep.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Suspicious logins: impossible travel and MFA push spam
question: Which single field most changes the urgency of a push-storm alert?
options: Whether a push was approved after the storm
The number of pushes
The user's department
The phone's operating system
explain: Many denied pushes mean the attacker has the password but not the account yet: urgent, but contained (reset the password). An approval after a storm means the attacker may already hold a session, so revoke it now and find out what it did.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Ransomware precursors, and deciding fast: Colonial Pipeline
question: At 02:14 a shadow-copy deletion alert fires on a file server. No other alerts yet. The on-call IR lead is asleep. What is the best first move?
options: Wait until the morning shift and investigate then
Restore the shadow copies
Email the server owner and wait for a reply
Page the IR lead now, isolate the host if the playbook pre-authorises it, and start collecting the process tree and the account that ran the command
explain: Recovery tampering is a late-stage precursor, and encryption may be minutes away. Paging at 02:14 is exactly what on-call exists for. Pre-authorised isolation buys time; evidence about the process and account tells IR how far the intrusion has spread.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: SOAR playbooks: what to automate and what to keep human
question: Which step is the best candidate for full automation with no human approval?
options: Disabling the CEO's account on a push-storm alert
Isolating a production database server on an EDR alert
Adding identity, asset owner and past-alert context to every new identity alert
Closing alerts whose destination IP has a benign reputation
explain: Enrichment is repetitive, fast and harmless if it errs: it only adds context for a human. The others are high-impact (CEO account, production database) or rely on reputation data that is easily wrong (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Warnings people heed: browser warnings and opinionated design
question: Chrome's 2013 SSL warning had 70.2% clickthrough while its malware warning had 23.2%. What does Akhawe and Felt's comparison mostly show?
options: Chrome users are more reckless than Firefox users
The presentation and context of a warning strongly change behaviour
SSL errors are always harmless
Malware warnings are shown less often
explain: Chrome users heeded most malware warnings, and Firefox users heeded most SSL warnings. The large difference for one warning type in one browser points at that warning's design and context, not at the users.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Voice clones and deepfake meetings: when seeing is not believing
question: Why is a video call that the requester arranges weak evidence of identity, even if the faces look right?
options: Because the requester controls that channel, so its content can be fabricated end to end
Because video calls are always encrypted
Because faces cannot be seen clearly on video
Because video calls are not recorded
explain: In the Arup case every participant except the victim was generated. Evidence produced inside a channel the attacker set up proves nothing about identity; only an independent channel does.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Physical security in layers: zones, CPTED and access rules
question: A company removes the bushes outside its ground-floor windows and lights the car park. Which CPTED approach is that?
options: Territorial behaviour
Natural access control
Natural surveillance
Target hardening with locks
explain: Clearing sightlines and adding light lets people see and be seen, which is natural surveillance. Access control steers movement; territorial behaviour marks ownership.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Testing the people layer: rules of engagement, ethics and metrics
question: A phishing simulation's click rate falls from 12% to 6%, and its report rate falls from 40% to 15%. Which reading is best?
options: The programme is working, since fewer people click
Reporting has collapsed, which removes the early warning the SOC depends on; investigate why
Click rate is the only metric that matters
The lure was too easy
explain: Fewer clicks with far fewer reports can mean people ignore or delete suspicious mail out of fear or fatigue. The report is what lets responders contain a real campaign.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: The sparse autoencoder: a wide, sparse dictionary for activations
question: You train an SAE on layer 6 residual-stream activations of your GPT. Which statement is true?
options: The GPT's weights are updated so its neurons become monosemantic
The SAE has fewer hidden units than d_model so it compresses the activations
The SAE is trained on next-token cross-entropy only
The GPT is frozen; the SAE learns a wider, sparse re-description of the saved layer 6 vectors
explain: The SAE is a separate model trained on stored activations. It is overcomplete (M much larger than d) and trained with a reconstruction plus sparsity objective, not by changing the language model.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Six sensors and a blank map: interpolation as weighted averaging
question: A colleague says nearest neighbor is safest because it never invents values that were not measured. What is the main weakness of the resulting map?
options: It cannot be computed without a fitted variogram
It is discontinuous: the value jumps at Voronoi cell borders even when the true field is smooth
It always returns the global mean far from sensors
It gives every sensor the same weight
explain: Nearest neighbor copies the closest reading, so the map is a set of flat Voronoi tiles with steps at the borders. It needs no model, and far from sensors it still copies the nearest one rather than the mean.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Which map to trust: leave-one-out cross-validation
question: You have 5,000 weather stations and need a 1 km map nightly. Global ordinary kriging is too slow. Which change keeps most of kriging's benefits?
options: Switch to nearest neighbor
Krige from a local neighborhood of the nearest few dozen stations per target, using a variogram fitted once on all stations
Drop the variogram and set all weights to 1/5000
Use IDW with p = 0
explain: Local neighborhoods (like scikit-gstat's max_points or RBFInterpolator's neighbors) make each solve small. Distant stations get negligible weight beyond the range anyway, so the map changes little while cost drops sharply.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: How many tokens per round, and what speedup to expect
question: Which change raises the maximum achievable speedup when the draft is free (c = 0)?
options: Increasing gamma beyond 20
Lowering the target's temperature has no effect
Using a bigger GPU for the draft
Raising alpha, because the speedup is capped by 1/(1 - alpha)
explain: With c = 0 the speedup is the expected tokens per pass, bounded by 1/(1 - alpha) however large gamma gets. Only better acceptance raises the cap; lower temperature usually helps because it sharpens both distributions.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Whisper: a transformer over 30-second spectrogram windows
question: Whisper's timestamp tokens are quantized to the native resolution. A word starts at 1.234 s. What is the closest timestamp the model can emit?
explain: Each encoder position covers 20 ms (30 s / 1500), and timestamp tokens are on the same 20 ms grid: ..., 1.22, 1.24, ... The nearest grid point to 1.234 s is 1.24 s. Finer word timings need extra machinery, such as the cross-attention alignment the openai/whisper code offers for word timestamps.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The stack: memory that frees itself when a function returns
question: A function returns `&x`, where `x` is one of its local variables. The caller reads the pointer immediately and gets the right value, but after calling `printf` it reads garbage. Why?
options: The compiler moved x to the heap, and printf freed it
x's frame was released on return; printf's own frame reused those stack bytes
Reading a stack variable from another function always raises SIGSEGV
The red zone is cleared by the kernel on every return
explain: Returning only moves `rsp` back up; the bytes are not erased, so an immediate read may look fine. The next call (here `printf`) pushes its frame into the same addresses and overwrites them. No fault occurs because the memory is still mapped, which is what makes this bug so sneaky. The red zone is never cleared by the kernel.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Page faults: lazy allocation, copy-on-write and overcommit
question: A machine has 16 GiB of RAM, no swap and `vm.overcommit_memory = 0`. Processes A and B each malloc 12 GiB and each writes only its first 1 GiB. What most likely happens?
options: B's malloc returns NULL because 24 GiB exceeds RAM
Both mallocs succeed and both run normally: only touched pages use RAM
Both succeed, then the OOM killer immediately kills one of them
The kernel zeroes 24 GiB at malloc time and the machine swaps
explain: The default heuristic only rejects a single request bigger than RAM plus swap; 12 GiB is not, and it does not add up other processes' reservations. Frames are allocated on first touch, so about 2 GiB of RAM is used. Only if A and B actually wrote more than RAM holds would the OOM killer step in.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Where to add it, at which tokens, and how hard
question: A vector extracted at layer 6 of a 48-layer model works well at c = 4. A colleague adds the same vector at layer 40 with c = 4 and sees almost no effect. What is the most likely explanation?
options: At layer 40 the residual stream is much larger, so the same c is a much smaller relative push, and the concept may be represented differently there
Steering vectors only work in the first half of a network
Adding at a later layer reverses the sign of the vector
The model detects the vector and removes it
explain: Residual norms grow with depth, so a fixed-size vector becomes relatively small; on top of that, a direction found at layer 6 need not be the direction the concept uses at layer 40. Extract and inject at the same layer, and sweep c relative to the local norm.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Ingest: MQTT at the edge, a Kafka log in the middle
question: A topic has 4 partitions and a consumer group with 6 consumers. How many consumers receive records?
options: 6: Kafka splits each partition across consumers
1: only the group leader reads
4: each partition goes to exactly one consumer in the group, so 2 sit idle
12: every consumer reads every partition
explain: Kafka assigns each partition to exactly one consumer within a group. With more consumers than partitions, the extras get nothing. Parallelism within a group is capped by the partition count.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Why recurrence was the bottleneck for sequence models
question: Which problem of the basic RNN encoder-decoder did Bahdanau-style attention fix, and which did it leave in place?
options: It fixed sequential computation but kept the fixed-length vector
It removed the fixed-length vector bottleneck but kept the sequential recurrent chain
It fixed both, which is why the Transformer only changed the training recipe
It fixed neither; it only made the model more interpretable
explain: The decoder could now look at every encoder state through a weighted sum, so the single fixed vector stopped being a bottleneck. The encoder and decoder were still RNNs, so computation inside a sequence stayed sequential. The Transformer removed that remaining chain.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Positional encoding and the full encoder-decoder stack
question: You remove the positional encodings from a trained encoder and feed it "dog bites man" and "man bites dog". What happens to the encoder output for the token "man"?
options: It is identical in both sentences
It differs, because attention weights depend on which tokens are nearby
It differs, because the FFN processes positions in order
It becomes all zeros
explain: Without positional information, self-attention and the position-wise FFN are permutation equivariant. Both sentences contain the same three tokens, so "man" gets the same output in each. That is why order must be injected explicitly.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Training recipe, quadratic cost and what changed since 2017
question: You increase the context length of a model from 4,096 to 16,384 tokens and keep d fixed. Roughly how does the score-matrix work per layer change?
options: It grows about 4 times, like the FFN
It grows about 16 times, while the FFN work grows about 4 times
It stays the same because heads run in parallel
It grows about 2 times
explain: Score work scales with n^2: (16384/4096)^2 = 16. The FFN and projections scale with n, so they grow 4 times. Parallel heads change wall-clock time, not the amount of work.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: BM25 in Lucene and Elasticsearch: fields, tuning, limits
question: An Elasticsearch index has 5 shards and a rare term that happens to be concentrated in one shard. Why might the same document get a slightly different BM25 score than in a single-shard index?
options: IDF and avgdl are computed from per-shard statistics by default
BM25 uses random tie-breaking
k1 is divided by the number of shards
Norms are only stored on the primary shard
explain: Lucene computes N, n_t and avgdl from the index it searches. In Elasticsearch each shard is a separate Lucene index, and the default query_then_fetch search type scores with local, per-shard term and document frequencies. Skewed terms then get different IDFs per shard. The dfs_query_then_fetch search type gathers global frequencies first, at extra cost.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Assemble model.py and check it against GPT-2's real weights
question: After loading GPT-2's weights, your logits differ from Hugging Face's by at most 0.08 and every argmax agrees. Which cause fits best?
options: A missing transpose on attn.c_proj
The MLP uses exact GELU while GPT-2 was trained with the tanh approximation
Weight tying is missing
The causal mask is upper-triangular
explain: The two GELU formulas differ by a few ten-thousandths per activation, which adds up to small logit differences that rarely change the argmax; that is what we measured (0.080). A missing transpose gave a difference of 161.7 and degenerate text, and a flipped mask would leak the future and change the logits wildly.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Making it fast: TF32, bfloat16, torch.compile, fused attention and DDP
question: A run of GPT-2 124M processes 400,000 tokens per second on one GPU with a 989 TFLOP/s bf16 peak. Using 855 million FLOPs per token, what is its MFU?
options: About 86%
About 4%
About 35%
About 12%
explain: 400,000 x 855e6 = 3.42e14 FLOP/s, and 3.42e14 / 9.89e14 = 0.35. MFU compares useful model FLOPs to the hardware peak, the same calculation as for the A100 run.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Many inputs: partial derivatives and the gradient vector
question: A model has 7 billion parameters and a scalar loss. How many numbers are in the gradient of the loss?
options: 1, because the loss is a single number
7 billion, one partial derivative per parameter
About 49 billion billion (7 billion squared), one per pair of parameters
It depends on the batch size
explain: The gradient has one entry per input to the function: here, one partial derivative per parameter. Pairs of parameters appear in the matrix of second derivatives (the Hessian: each entry differentiates one partial derivative again with respect to another parameter; lesson 7), which is far too large to form for such models.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Jacobians: derivatives of vector-valued functions
question: A linear layer maps 512 inputs to 256 outputs, $z = Wx + b$. What are the shapes of the Jacobian $\partial z/\partial x$ and of the gradient $\partial L/\partial W$ for a scalar loss $L$?
options: Both 512 x 256
Jacobian 256 x 512; dL/dW 256 x 512, the shape of W
Jacobian 256 x 512; dL/dW 512 x 1
Jacobian 512 x 512; dL/dW 256 x 256
explain: The Jacobian has one row per output (256) and one column per input (512), and it equals $W$, which is $256 \times 512$. The gradient of a scalar loss with respect to $W$ has one entry per weight, so it matches $W$'s shape; it is the outer product of the 256-entry $\partial L/\partial z$ with the 512-entry $x$.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Expansion and quoting: why rm $f can delete the wrong files
question: In bash, `echo {1,2}-$((3+4))` prints what?
explain: Brace expansion runs first and makes two words, `1-$((3+4))` and `2-$((3+4))`. Arithmetic expansion then evaluates each to 7.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Searching and transforming text: grep, regex, find, sed and awk
question: In a folder containing `a.txt` and `b.txt`, `find . -name *.txt` fails with an error. Why?
options: find does not accept globs after -name
-name needs the full path rather than a pattern
The shell expands `*.txt` to `a.txt b.txt` before find runs, so find gets an extra argument it cannot parse
find refuses to search the current directory
explain: Expansion happens before the command runs (lesson 3). find receives `-name a.txt b.txt`; -name takes exactly one pattern, so `b.txt` is a stray argument. `find . -name '*.txt'` passes the pattern through for find to match against every file name in the tree.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Learning word vectors by predicting their neighbours
question: With window $c = 2$, how many (center, context) pairs does the 6-word sentence *the cat sat on the mat* produce?
explain: Edge words have fewer neighbours: positions 0 and 5 get 2 context words each, positions 1 and 4 get 3, positions 2 and 3 get 4. That is 2 + 3 + 4 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 18. The naive 6 x 4 = 24 forgets that the window is cut off at the sentence edges.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: What the geometry means: cosine, analogies and PMI
question: A teammate reports that *king - man + woman* returns *king* in your system. What is the best first check?
options: Retrain with a larger dimension
Switch from cosine to Euclidean distance
Whether the nearest-neighbour search excludes the three query words, as the original evaluation did
Increase the number of negative samples
explain: Returning an input word is the expected behaviour when inputs are not excluded: Nissim et al. measured 0.21 accuracy unconstrained vs 0.74 constrained on the same vectors.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Beyond words: autoencoders and the InfoNCE loss
question: A contrastive model is trained with InfoNCE over $N = 256$ candidates per anchor. What is the most mutual information, in nats, that the bound $\log N - L_N$ can certify, however good the encoder?
explain: $L_N \ge 0$, so $\log N - L_N \le \ln 256 = 5.545$ nats (8 bits). 1.386 is $\ln 4$, the limit for 4 candidates; to certify more, use more candidates.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Prefill and decode: FLOPs and bytes per generated token
question: Which change most reduces time to first token for a request with a very long prompt?
options: Faster HBM only
More math throughput (or splitting prefill across GPUs), since prefill is compute-bound
A larger decode batch
Lowering the number of output tokens
explain: TTFT is dominated by prefill (plus any queueing), and prefill of many tokens is compute-bound. Output length affects total latency, not TTFT.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Bits, bytes and hex: how numbers are stored
question: An `int` holding `0x12345678` is stored at address 0x100 on x86-64. Which byte is at address 0x100?
explain: x86-64 is little-endian: the least significant byte, 0x78, goes at the lowest address, followed by 0x56, 0x34 and 0x12 at 0x101 to 0x103. A big-endian machine would put 0x12 first.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why real CPUs beat the simple loop: pipelines and prediction
question: A profile shows a hot loop whose `if` on input data is mispredicted about half the time. Which change is most likely to help?
options: Add a few more instructions before the if so the CPU has time to think
Make the outcome predictable or branch-free, for example sort or group the data, or let the compiler use a conditional move
Split the loop across two functions
Turn off out-of-order execution
explain: The cost comes from flushing the pipeline on each wrong guess. Removing the guess (a conditional move) or making it right almost every time (sorted or grouped data) removes the penalty. Extra instructions or function boundaries do not make the direction any easier to predict.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Pretraining: next-token loss over trillions of tokens
question: Using C of about 6ND, a 7B-parameter model trained on 2 trillion tokens needs roughly how many FLOPs?
explain: 6 x 7e9 x 2e12 = 8.4e22. The rule ignores attention's context-length term, which Kaplan et al. note is small when the model width is large relative to the context.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Policy gradients: how a score becomes a gradient
question: A policy samples response C, which has reward -1, with probabilities p = (0.426, 0.258, 0.316) over A, B, C. Without a baseline, how does this one sample move the three logits under gradient ascent?
options: It raises all three logits, because the gradient of a probability is always positive
It lowers C's logit and raises A's and B's, since r times (onehot(C) - p) = (0.426, 0.258, -0.684)
It raises C's logit, because C was the response sampled
It leaves the logits unchanged, because negative rewards give no gradient
explain: The sample's contribution is r(C) times (onehot(C) - p) = -1 times (-0.426, -0.258, 0.684). Ascent lowers C's logit by the largest amount and lifts the others. A negative reward acts like a push away from what was sampled.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: From grep to the inverted index
question: Why does an inverted index keep each postings list sorted by docID?
options: So that the most relevant documents come first
So two lists can be intersected by walking them once, side by side
Because docIDs must be unique
So the dictionary can be binary searched
explain: A single global sort order lets the query engine merge two lists in one linear pass (lesson 3). Sorting by docID says nothing about relevance; ranking is a separate step. Binary search over the dictionary concerns terms, not postings.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Ranking with vectors and cosine similarity
question: Why do engines store the integer tf in each posting instead of the final tf-idf weight?
options: Because idf depends on df and N, which change as documents are added, and an integer is cheaper to store than a float
Because floats cannot be sorted
Because tf-idf weights are always integers anyway
Because cosine similarity ignores idf
explain: idf is a collection-wide statistic, so a stored tf-idf float would go stale every time the collection changes. A small integer tf also compresses far better than a float. The engine combines tf with the current idf at query time.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Addresses and pointers: what int *p actually stores
question: Given `int x = 5; int *p = &x; int **pp = &p; **pp = 9;`, what is the value of x?
options: 5, because only pp was assigned
It is undefined behavior
The address of p
explain: *pp is the object pp points to, which is p. **pp follows p one more step, reaching x. Assigning 9 through it writes into x. All of this is well defined because every pointer points to a live object of the right type.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Object lifetimes: automatic, static and malloc'd memory
question: After `free(p);` the program later runs `free(p);` again. What does the C standard say happens?
options: The second call does nothing, like free(NULL)
The behavior is undefined
free returns an error code
The memory is freed twice, which is harmless
explain: free on a block that has already been deallocated is explicitly undefined behavior. Only a null pointer is a guaranteed no-op, which is why some code writes `free(p); p = NULL;`.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Undefined behavior, and the tools that catch it
question: An ASan report says `heap-use-after-free ... READ of size 4 ... in main uaf.c:7` and `freed by thread T0 here: ... in main uaf.c:6`. What is the bug?
options: Line 7 reads through a pointer whose block was freed on line 6
Line 6 frees a pointer that malloc never returned
Line 7 reads an uninitialized local variable on the stack
The program ran out of heap memory
explain: ASan reports the bad access (line 7), plus where the block was freed (line 6) and allocated. Reading 4 bytes after free is a use after free. The fix is to finish using the data before freeing it, or not to free it yet.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Moves, Copy and clone: why let s2 = s1 kills s1
options: None; `drop` is special and can be called twice
`drop(s)`, because the first iteration moves `s` into `drop` and the second iteration uses a moved value
`for _ in 0..2`, because loops cannot capture Strings
explain: `drop` is an ordinary function taking its argument by value, so the first call moves `s`. The compiler sees the loop can run again and reports E0382 (use of moved value). This is a double free the compiler caught.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Lifetimes: tying a returned reference to its inputs
question: Which signature compiles **without** explicit lifetime annotations?
options: `fn pick(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str`
`fn make() -> &str`
`fn get(&self, key: &str) -> &str` (a method)
explain: Rule 3: the output takes the lifetime of `&self`. Options 1 and 4 have two input lifetimes and no receiver, and option 2 has no input lifetime at all, so elision cannot fill in the output in any of them (E0106).

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A vector is a list of numbers and an arrow at the same time
question: You store 1,000 user profiles, each with 32 numeric features, as vectors. Which statement is right?
options: Each profile is a vector in R^1000
You cannot add two profiles because their features have different meanings
Each profile is a vector in R^32, and you can add two profiles component by component
Each feature is a vector in R^32
explain: Each profile has 32 components, so it lives in $\mathbb{R}^{32}$. The math allows adding any two vectors of the same dimension; whether the sum is *meaningful* depends on the features, but averaging profiles (add, then scale by 1/2) is a common and legal operation.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Span, independence and rank: what a matrix can reach
question: Three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$: $[1,0]$, $[0,1]$ and $[1,1]$. Which statement is right?
options: They are linearly independent, because no two of them are parallel
Their span is 3-dimensional, one dimension per vector
They are linearly dependent, and their span is the whole plane
They are dependent, so their span is only a line
explain: $[1,1] = [1,0] + [0,1]$, so the set is dependent, but the first two already reach every point of the plane. No two being parallel is not enough for independence. The plane has dimension 2, so no set of 3 vectors in it can be independent, and no span inside it can be 3-dimensional.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Tensors, batches and broadcasting: shapes in real code
question: Arrays of shape (8, 1, 6) and (7, 6) are added. What is the result's shape?
options: An error, because they have different numbers of axes
explain: Pad the shorter shape on the left: (1, 7, 6). Compare from the right: 6 and 6 match, 1 and 7 give 7, 8 and 1 give 8. Result (8, 7, 6). Different numbers of axes are fine; missing axes count as size 1.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Many features: linear regression in matrix form and feature scaling
question: A model uses income in USD (values around 50,000) and age in years (around 40). Gradient descent needs a tiny learning rate and the age weight barely moves. What is the best first fix?
options: Use a much larger learning rate
Drop the age feature
Train for more epochs
Standardize both features using training-set means and standard deviations
explain: Income's huge scale makes its curvature, and so the largest Hessian eigenvalue, enormous, which caps the safe learning rate; age then crawls. Standardizing equalizes the scales. A larger rate would diverge along the income direction, and more epochs only wait out the crawl.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Validation and penalties: choosing lambda, L2 and L1
question: With SGD and learning rate 0.1, an L2 term $\lambda\lVert w\rVert^2$ with $\lambda = 0.0005$ shrinks each weight by what factor before the gradient step?
explain: The step is $w \leftarrow (1 - 2\eta\lambda)w - \eta\nabla L$, and $2 \times 0.1 \times 0.0005 = 0.0001$, so the factor is $0.9999$. Note the factor 2 from differentiating $\lambda w^2$; many libraries define the penalty with a $\tfrac{1}{2}$ to cancel it.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Build it: a complete training loop in NumPy
question: Someone runs this code with lam = 1.0 instead of 0.001. Validation loss stalls at about 0.63 and the weights end near (0.13, 0.13). What happened?
options: The penalty dominates the loss, shrinking the weights so much that predictions stay near 0.5: underfitting
The model overfits because lambda is large
Early stopping fired too late
The data were not shuffled
explain: With $\lambda = 1$ the term $\lambda\lVert w\rVert^2$ outweighs the gain from fitting, so the weights stay tiny, every $p$ stays near 0.5, and the loss stays close to $\ln 2 = 0.693$. Strong regularization trades variance for bias, and here bias wins. Choose $\lambda$ on validation data.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The chain rule on a computational graph
question: In the forward pass $m = \max(a, b)$ with $a = 4$ and $b = 1$. The upstream gradient is $\partial L/\partial m = 2$. What are $\partial L/\partial a$ and $\partial L/\partial b$?
options: 1 and 1
2 and 2
2 and 0
1.6 and 0.4, split by size
explain: Max routes the gradient: only the input that won (a = 4) affects m, so it gets the full upstream gradient 2. Nudging b slightly does not change m at all, so its gradient is 0.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradients through depth: vanishing, exploding and unlucky seeds
question: A layer has 256 inputs and 64 outputs. Which weight variance does Glorot initialisation use, and which condition does each width come from?
options: $1/256$: only the forward pass matters
$2/320 = 1/160$: 256 from keeping activations steady going forward, 64 from keeping errors steady going backward
$2/64$: He initialisation for the output width
$1/64$: only the backward pass matters
explain: Forward, a unit sums 256 inputs, so steady activations need $256\,v = 1$. Backward, BP2 sums over the 64 units each input feeds, so steady errors need $64\,v = 1$. Glorot averages the widths: $v = 2/(256 + 64) = 1/160$.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: CPU scheduling: turnaround time versus response time
question: Three 5-second jobs arrive together. You switch from SJF to round robin with a 1 s slice. What happens to average turnaround and average response time?
options: Both improve
Turnaround gets worse (10 s to 14 s) and response gets better (5 s to 1 s)
Turnaround improves and response gets worse
Both stay the same because the total work is unchanged
explain: RR starts every job almost immediately, so average response drops from 5 s to 1 s. But it interleaves the jobs, so all of them finish near the end: 13, 14 and 15 s, averaging 14 s versus SJF's 10 s. Fairness over short time scales costs turnaround.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Waiting for something: condition variables and semaphores
question: A bounded buffer has one producer and two consumers, one condition variable, and consumers that check `if (count == 0)` before waiting. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing: with a lock held, if and while behave the same
A woken consumer can find the buffer already emptied by the other consumer and call get() on an empty buffer
The producer can overwrite a full buffer even with one consumer
The program deadlocks because wait() keeps the mutex
explain: Under Mesa semantics a wakeup is only a hint. Between the producer's signal and Tc1 running, Tc2 can take the item. With if, Tc1 does not re-check and calls get() on an empty buffer. wait() releases the mutex while sleeping, so the last option is wrong.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Files and directories: the API and how vsfs finds your data
question: With nothing cached, each directory fitting in one block, and the superblock in memory, how many disk reads does `open("/a/b/c")` cost?
explain: Root inode, root data, a's inode, a's data, b's inode, b's data, and finally c's inode: 7 reads. open() reads the target's inode but not its data; the data is read by later read() calls.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Probability by counting outcomes, and what conditioning does
question: You flip a fair coin twice. Let A = "first flip is heads" and B = "the two flips match". Are A and B independent?
options: No, because B depends on the first flip
Yes: P(A and B) = 1/4 = P(A) P(B)
No, because A and B can both happen
It cannot be determined without more data
explain: P(A) = 1/2, P(B) = 2/4 = 1/2 (HH or TT), and P(A and B) = P(HH) = 1/4 = P(A)P(B). Even though B is defined using the first flip, it is independent of A. Independence is checked with numbers, not by whether one event is mentioned in the other's definition.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Why averages are stable: the law of large numbers and the CLT
question: Batch size 64 gives a gradient-estimate standard deviation of s (per coordinate, i.i.d. examples). Approximately what does batch size 256 give?
options: s, since batch size does not affect noise
explain: The mini-batch gradient is an average of per-example gradients, so its standard deviation scales as 1/sqrt(batch). Four times the batch gives sqrt(4) = 2 times less noise, so s/2. The variance falls by 4.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayesian estimation: priors, posteriors and MAP
question: Prior Beta(3, 3). You observe 2 heads and 6 tails. What are the posterior and its MAP estimate?
options: Beta(5, 9), MAP 1/3
Beta(2, 6), MAP 0.25
Beta(5, 9), MAP 0.25, the same as the MLE
Beta(3, 3), since one small sample does not change the prior
explain: Add heads to a and tails to b: Beta(3 + 2, 3 + 6) = Beta(5, 9). MAP = (5 - 1) / (5 + 9 - 2) = 4/12 = 1/3, pulled from the MLE of 0.25 toward the prior's 0.5.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Counting training compute: C is about 6ND
question: Your budget is fixed. You decide to make the model 3 times larger than planned. What must happen to the number of training tokens?
options: It stays the same, compute depends only on N
It must triple
It must drop to one third
It must drop to one ninth
explain: With $C \approx 6ND$ fixed, $D = C/(6N)$, so tripling N cuts D to one third. Compute depends on both knobs; nothing about the product is squared.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Kaplan vs Chinchilla: why 2020-era models were undertrained
question: Which is the best summary of the Kaplan vs Chinchilla disagreement?
options: Chinchilla showed loss does not follow power laws
They agree that loss is a power law, but differ on how to split compute; replications trace Kaplan's split to experimental setup
Kaplan used more compute so its result is more reliable
The difference is only because they used different tokenizers
explain: Both papers find smooth power-law trends. The disagreement is the compute-optimal exponent (0.73 vs about 0.5), and later work explains it by schedule, parameter counting, small scale and optimizer details. Kaplan actually used smaller models than Chinchilla.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Precision, recall, and why accuracy is useless for search
question: A query has exactly 3 relevant documents in the qrels. A perfect system ranks all 3 first. What are its P@10 and R@10?
explain: Recall is 3/3 = 1.0 because every relevant document is retrieved. Precision at 10 counts all 10 slots, and only 3 can ever be relevant, so it is 0.3 even for a perfect ranking. This is why P@k is hard to average across queries with different numbers of relevant documents.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: From token vectors to one sentence vector: pooling and cosine
question: Your vectors are L2-normalized at indexing time and queries are normalized too. A teammate switches the scoring function from cosine to dot product to save time. What happens to the ranking?
options: It is identical, because for unit vectors the dot product equals the cosine
It changes, because dot product favors longer documents
It reverses
It becomes random
explain: Cosine divides the dot product by the two lengths. When both lengths are 1, that division does nothing, so the scores and the ranking are identical. This is exactly why normalizing once is standard practice.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Training BPE: count adjacent pairs, merge the top one, repeat
question: Starting from the initial corpus, suppose newest appeared 9 times instead of 6 (everything else unchanged). Which pair would be merged first?
options: (e, s), still tied with (s, t) and (t, _) at 12
(l, o), because low is the most frequent word
(w, e), which rises to 11
(n, e), because newest is now the most frequent word
explain: Each of (e, s), (s, t), (t, _) becomes $9 + 3 = 12$, and (w, e) becomes $9 + 2 = 11$. The top count is a three-way tie at 12, and the first-seen rule picks (e, s). Word frequency alone does not decide: (l, o) gets 7 and (n, e) gets 9.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Special tokens, chat templates and prompt boundaries
question: A service builds each prompt as system_text + user_text and encodes it with `enc.encode(prompt, allowed_special="all")`. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; allowed_special only changes how decoding works
It is slower, but the ids are identical either way
It raises ValueError on every prompt
A user who types a special string such as <|endoftext|> gets the real control token, so their text can end the document or fake structure the model trusts
explain: allowed_special="all" turns every special string in the text into its control id, including strings typed by users. Allow special tokens only in text you wrote, and encode user text with the defaults (which raise) or with disallowed_special=() so it stays plain text.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Initialization: keeping signals alive through 30 layers
question: Why does He initialization use 2 / fan-in rather than Xavier's 1 / fan-in (equal fans) for ReLU layers?
options: ReLU doubles the gradient on the positive side
The factor 2 accounts for the bias term
ReLU zeroes about half of a symmetric pre-activation, halving the mean square, and the factor 2 cancels that
Larger weights train faster, so 2 is a safe speed-up
explain: With zero-mean symmetric pre-activations, ReLU keeps only the positive half, so the average of $\mathrm{relu}(z)^2$ is $\mathrm{Var}(z)/2$. Multiplying Var(w) by 2 restores a per-layer factor of exactly 1.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Mixed precision: fp16, bf16 and loss scaling
question: Your gradients include many values around 1e-9 and you want to avoid a loss scaler. Which format works, and what does it give up?
options: fp16, because subnormals reach down past 1e-9
bf16: fp32's exponent range keeps 1e-9 representable, at the cost of only 7 mantissa bits (spacing 0.0078 near 1)
fp16, because it has more mantissa bits than bf16
Either one: both have 8 exponent bits
explain: fp16's smallest positive number is 2^-24, about 6e-8, so 1e-9 rounds to 0 unless the loss is scaled. bf16 keeps fp32's 8 exponent bits, so range is not the problem; precision is, which is why the weights stay in fp32.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Instrumenting a run: gradient norms, update ratios, activation stats
question: A run's loss sits at 2.30 (10 classes) for 300 steps. Every layer's update-to-weight ratio is about 1e-8, and the activation std drops about 8x per layer. Most likely cause?
options: Weights initialized far too small, so the signal and gradients vanish
A learning rate 30x too high
model.eval() was never called
Dropout is too strong
explain: A constant ln 10 loss means the network predicts uniformly. The per-layer scale collapse matches lesson 1's analysis of a too-small init, and ratios of 1e-8 mean the weights are effectively frozen. A too-high rate gives large ratios and climbing gradient norms instead.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Building the graph: insertion and the neighbor heuristic
question: Which change increases index build time but leaves query-time cost per ef roughly the same?
options: Raising ef at query time
Raising ef_construction
Raising M
Raising the dimension d
explain: ef_construction only controls the beam width during inserts. M also raises query cost because every expanded node has more neighbors to score; d makes every distance more expensive; ef is the query knob itself.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Install scripts: why installing a package runs its code
question: Which of these runs a third-party package's own code on your machine before your application ever imports it?
options: Installing an npm package that has a postinstall script, with scripts enabled
Reading the package's README on the registry website
Running npm ls
Installing a pure-Python wheel with pip
explain: Lifecycle scripts run during install. A wheel is unpacked without running package code (though a .pth file it installs runs at the next Python start).

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Build system compromise: SolarWinds, CCleaner and 3CX
question: SUNSPOT replaced a source file only while MsBuild was running and restored it afterwards. Which check would most likely have exposed it?
options: Verifying the code-signing signature on the shipped DLL (dynamic-link library, a Windows code file)
Code review of the git repository
Running unit tests
Rebuilding the same commit on an independent builder and comparing hashes
explain: The repository was clean and the signature was genuine. Only something that compares the build output against an independent build of the same source sees the difference.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Signing artifacts: from long-lived keys to Sigstore
question: Why does keyless signing reduce the damage of a CI compromise compared with a GPG key stored as a CI secret?
options: Fulcio scans artifacts for malware before signing
There is no long-lived private key to steal; each key lives for one signature, and every signing event is publicly logged
Keyless signatures do not need verification
Sigstore signatures cannot be forged even by the signer
explain: An attacker inside the job could still sign during that run, but they cannot walk away with a key that works for months, and their signing is visible in Rekor. Compare HashiCorp's forced key rotation after Codecov.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: xz-utils I: two years of patient social engineering
question: Which control would most directly have stopped Jia Tan from shipping 5.6.0 alone?
options: Running unit tests in CI
Signing release tarballs
Requiring a second maintainer to review and approve every release and the release archive contents
Using SHA-256 instead of CRC in xz
explain: The releases were signed and tests passed. A second, independent person checking that the release archive matched the reviewed git tree is the control aimed at a single trusted insider, which SLSA's Source track formalises as required review.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Language models: decoding cuts the tail, scaling stalls
question: You generate 10x more synthetic training text from the same teacher with top-p 0.9. Under the tail-cutting model, when does this stop improving the student?
options: Never: error keeps falling as a power law in T
Once T exceeds roughly k to the power beta, where k is the effective tail cut; after that error plateaus at the missing tail mass
Immediately: synthetic data never helps
Only when the teacher's perplexity exceeds the student's
explain: Data from a tail-cut generator only teaches the head of the distribution. Once the student has learned the head, the remaining error is the mass of the items it never sees, and more samples from the same generator cannot reveal them.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Using synthetic data well: filter, diversify, anchor
question: A lab wants its 2027 pretraining mix to stay anchored to human text. Which plan does this lesson support best?
options: Keep pre-LLM snapshots and other known-human sources permanently in the mix, and treat classifier or watermark filtering of new crawls as an extra layer
Rely on an AI-text classifier to remove all model-written pages from new crawls, then drop the old snapshots to save space
Rely on watermarks, since every model that writes web text embeds one
Ignore provenance, since accumulating any data at all prevents every form of collapse
explain: Detectors can be evaded by paraphrasing and are bounded by how close AI text is to human text, and watermarks cover only cooperating generators. Known-human data kept permanently is the anchor that does not depend on detection. Accumulation bounds error but does not by itself protect the tails.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
